lessons.title: Hello, Rust!
lessons.body:
Think of a brand-new coffee machine: it does nothing until you press the ON button. In Rust, that ON button is the main function — every program starts there, always.

Here is the smallest possible Rust program:

```rust
fn main() {
    println!("Hello, world!");
}
```

Reading it line by line:

• fn main() — "here is a function named main". When you run the program, Rust presses this button first.
• println!("...") — prints one line of text to the screen. The ! at the end means it is a macro: a little code-writing helper, not a normal function. Don't worry about the difference yet — just remember: printing needs the !.
• The ; is a full stop. Every instruction ends with one, like sentences in English.
• The { } braces wrap the function's body — everything it does goes between them.

How do you run it? With Cargo — Rust's kitchen manager. It fetches ingredients (libraries), builds the dish, and serves it:

```rust
cargo new my_app   // start a new project
cargo run          // build it AND run it
```

That is genuinely all of it: programs start at main, instructions end with ;, printing uses println!, and cargo run brings it to life.

lessons.title: Variables & Mutability
lessons.body:
A variable is a labeled jar that holds a value. In most languages you can swap the contents anytime. In Rust, jars are SEALED by default — once filled, the contents never change:

```rust
let x = 5;  // a sealed jar labeled x
x = 6;      // ❌ error! can't refill a sealed jar
```

Want a refillable jar? Say so up front with mut (short for "mutable" = changeable):

```rust
let mut score = 0;  // refillable jar
score += 10;        // ✅ totally fine
```

Why sealed by default? Because if most jars CAN'T change, you never have to wonder "did something secretly modify this while I wasn't looking?" A whole family of bugs simply disappears.

Two more jar tricks:

```rust
// engraved in stone: never changes,
// type must be written out
const MAX_PLAYERS: u32 = 100;

// "shadowing": a NEW jar takes over the label
let spaces = "   ";        // jar of text
let spaces = spaces.len(); // new jar, now a number: 3
```

Shadowing looks like cheating, but notice: you never changed the old jar. You made a brand-new one and moved the label over — even a different type is allowed.

lessons.title: Data Types
lessons.body:
Rust wants to know exactly what kind of thing is in every jar — a number? text? true/false? This is called being "statically typed", and it means typos and mix-ups get caught before the program ever runs.

For numbers, think container sizes:

• u8 — an egg cup: whole numbers 0 to 255 (the u means "unsigned" = no negatives)
• i32 — a lunchbox: the everyday default for whole numbers
• f64 — for decimals like 4.99 (f = floating point)

```rust
let age: u8 = 25;     // small whole number
let price = 4.99;     // has a decimal -> f64
let is_open = true;   // bool: true or false
let crab = '🦀';      // char: exactly ONE symbol
```

Usually you can skip the type — Rust looks at the value and figures it out (5 becomes i32, 4.99 becomes f64).

For grouping values, two basic containers:

```rust
// tuple: a small bundle of mixed things
let point = (3, 7);
let x = point.0;   // first item (dot + position)

// array: a fixed row of same-type things
let days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"];
let first = days[0];
```

One superpower to remember: Rust always checks array bounds. Ask for days[10] and Rust refuses — other languages might silently hand you garbage memory, which is how mysterious crashes are born.

lessons.title: Comments & Printing
lessons.body:
Code is read far more often than it is written — usually by you, six months later, wondering what past-you was thinking. Comments are notes to that future reader. Rust ignores them completely when building.

```rust
// A line comment — everything after // is just a note.

let speed = 60; // notes can sit at the end of a line too

/* Block comments
   stretch across many lines —
   handy for switching off code temporarily. */
```

There is a third, special kind: doc comments with THREE slashes. Tooling turns these into real documentation pages:

```rust
/// Adds two numbers together.
fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b }
```

Now the other half of this lesson: making println! say exactly what you want. Each {} is a hole that gets filled in:

```rust
let name = "Sam";
let score = 42;
println!("{name} scored {score}");   // Sam scored 42
```

You can name the holes inline like above, or feed values in order:

```rust
println!("{} + {} = {}", 2, 3, 2 + 3); // 2 + 3 = 5
```

Two formatting tricks worth knowing now:

```rust
println!("{:.2}", 3.14159);  // 3.14  — round to 2 decimals
println!("{:?}", (1, 2));    // (1, 2) — the "debug" view
```

A plain {} asks a value to print itself nicely; {:?} asks for a developer's-eye debug view — the one that works on tuples, vectors and the structs you are inspecting.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.body:
A function is a vending machine: you put something in (parameters), it gives something back (the return value). Same input, same output, every time.

```rust
fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
    a + b
}

let sum = add(2, 3); // sum is 5
```

Reading the "machine label":

• fn add — the machine is called add.
• (a: i32, b: i32) — the coin slots: it accepts two whole numbers. Rust insists you label every slot's type, so the machine's manual is always accurate.
• -> i32 — the arrow points at what comes OUT: a whole number.

Now the unusual part. Where is the return keyword? Rust has a neat rule:

The last line WITHOUT a semicolon is the return value.

```rust
fn f() -> i32 {
    let x = 3;
    x + 1     // no ; -> this is returned: 4
}
```

Add a semicolon to that last line and you break it: `x + 1;` becomes "calculate this and throw it away", the machine returns nothing, but the label promised an i32 — compile error. This trips up every beginner exactly once. Now it won't trip you.

(The return keyword does exist — for exiting early, like return 0; inside an if.)

lessons.title: Expressions vs Statements
lessons.body:
Rust quietly splits everything you write into two camps. Knowing which is which explains a whole pile of "why won't this compile?" moments.

A STATEMENT performs an action but gives back no value. Declaring a variable is a statement:

```rust
let x = 5;   // does something, produces nothing usable
```

That is why this is an error — there is no value to grab:

```rust
let y = (let x = 5);  // ❌ a statement has no value
```

An EXPRESSION evaluates to a value. Most things are expressions:

```rust
5 + 3        // evaluates to 8
x * 2        // evaluates to a number
"hi".len()   // evaluates to 2
```

Here is the surprising part: a BLOCK { } is an expression too. Its value is the last line — if that line has no semicolon:

```rust
let y = {
    let a = 3;
    a + 1        // no ; — this is the block's value
};               // y is 4
```

This single rule explains the function trick from before: the last line without a semicolon becomes the return value. It also explains the semicolon bug:

```rust
let z = {
    let a = 3;
    a + 1;       // WITH ; — value thrown away
};               // z is now () — "nothing"
```

The semicolon is the switch: it turns an expression into a statement, dropping the value. if, match and loop are all expressions too — which is exactly why you can put them on the right side of let.

lessons.title: Pattern Matching with match
lessons.body:
You met match briefly with control flow. It is so central to Rust that it deserves its own lesson — think of it as a super-powered switch that the compiler polices.

The shape: a value, then a list of patterns, each with an arm:

```rust
let dice = 3;
match dice {
    1 => println!("lowest"),
    6 => println!("jackpot!"),
    _ => println!("something between"),
}
```

Each pattern is checked top to bottom; the FIRST match wins, and only that arm runs.

A few powers that make match shine:

```rust
match n {
    0 => "zero",
    1 | 2 | 3 => "small",   // | means "or"
    4..=9 => "medium",       // an inclusive range
    _ => "large",            // catch-all
}
```

Like if, match is an EXPRESSION — every arm produces a value, so you can assign the whole thing:

```rust
let size = match n {
    0..=9 => "one digit",
    _ => "many digits",
};
```

The rule that makes match special: it must be EXHAUSTIVE. Cover every possible value or the program will not compile. Forgetting the `_` catch-all (or a case) is caught immediately — "the value 7 is not handled". This is the compiler refusing to let an unhandled case slip into production.

lessons.title: Numbers & Arithmetic
lessons.body:
Numbers feel simple until a program quietly gives a wrong answer at 2am. Rust makes the rules visible so that never happens silently.

Whole numbers come in labelled sizes. The letter says signed or unsigned, the number says how many bits:

```rust
let a: i32 = -5;   // i = signed (can be negative)
let b: u8  = 200;  // u = unsigned (0 and up), 8 bits: 0..=255
let big: i64 = 9_000_000_000; // _ are just visual separators
```

Decimals are floats, defaulting to f64:

```rust
let pi = 3.14159;       // f64
let half: f32 = 0.5;    // f32 — smaller, less precise
```

The everyday operators: + - * / and % (remainder). Two classic surprises:

```rust
println!("{}", 7 / 2);   // 3  — integer division drops the rest
println!("{}", 7 % 2);   // 1  — % gives the leftover
println!("{}", 7.0 / 2.0); // 3.5 — use floats for decimals
```

And the one Rust handles unusually well — OVERFLOW. A u8 maxes out at 255. Add 1 to 255 and other languages silently wrap to 0, breeding bugs. In Rust's debug builds your program PANICS instead, pointing right at the mistake:

```rust
let x: u8 = 255;
let y = x + 1;   // panic in debug: "attempt to add with overflow"
```

When wrapping is actually what you want, you ask for it by name: x.wrapping_add(1). Numbers carry handy methods too, like 2_i32.pow(10) for powers.

lessons.title: Casting Between Types
lessons.body:
Rust never mixes number types behind your back. Add an i32 to an f64 and it simply refuses — it wants you to say, on purpose, how to convert. The tool for that is the `as` keyword.

```rust
let whole = 5;            // i32
let fraction = 2.5;       // f64
let sum = whole as f64 + fraction;  // convert, THEN add -> 7.5
```

Without `as f64` that line would not compile. The conversion is explicit so the cost and the rounding are never hidden.

Going from a float to an integer TRUNCATES — it chops the decimals, it does not round:

```rust
let x = 9.9 as i32;   // 9, not 10  (the .9 is thrown away)
let y = -2.7 as i32;  // -2
```

Going to a smaller integer type keeps only what fits, which can surprise you:

```rust
let big = 300;
let small = big as u8;  // 300 doesn't fit 0..=255 -> wraps to 44
```

One type you will meet constantly is usize — the type Rust uses for sizes and indexes. Lengths come back as usize, so you often cast to compare or compute:

```rust
let len = "hello".len();      // usize
let n = len as i32 - 10;      // cast to do signed math
```

Rule of thumb: reach for `as` when you knowingly want a numeric conversion, and remember float-to-int chops rather than rounds. For everyday rounding, call .round() first: (9.9_f64).round() as i32 gives 10.

lessons.title: Strings: String vs &str
lessons.body:
Rust has two text types that confuse every newcomer. Once the distinction clicks, it stays clicked — so let us make it click.

&str (a "string slice") is a borrowed VIEW of text you do not own. Every literal in quotes is one, baked permanently into your program:

```rust
let greeting = "hello";   // type: &str — fixed, read-only
```

String is an OWNED, growable buffer that lives on the heap. You make one when you need to build or change text:

```rust
let mut name = String::from("Sam");  // owned, can grow
name.push_str(" Smith");             // now "Sam Smith"
```

The mental model: &str is a label you can read; String is a notebook you can write in. Converting between them is easy:

```rust
let owned: String = "hi".to_string();  // &str -> String
let view: &str = &owned;               // String -> &str (a borrow)
```

Joining text has two common tools:

```rust
let full = format!("{} {}", "Sam", "Smith"); // builds a new String
let a = String::from("foo");
let b = a + "bar";   // + consumes `a`, returns "foobar"
```

format! is the friendly one — it never steals its inputs and reads just like println!.

One gotcha to file away: .len() counts BYTES, not characters. Because Rust strings are UTF-8, an emoji or accented letter is several bytes. For counting actual characters, use .chars().count(). This is why you cannot index a string with s[0] — a byte is not always a character.

lessons.title: Boolean Logic
lessons.body:
Every decision a program makes comes down to true or false. The bool type holds exactly those two values — nothing else, no "truthy" numbers like in other languages.

```rust
let is_open = true;
let is_empty = false;
```

Three operators combine and flip booleans. Picture them as plain English:

AND — written && — true only when BOTH sides are true. "Is it warm AND sunny?"

```rust
let go_out = warm && sunny;   // both must hold
```

OR — written || — true when EITHER side is true. "Is it Saturday OR Sunday?"

```rust
let weekend = saturday || sunday;  // one is enough
```

NOT — written ! — flips a bool to its opposite. "It is NOT raining."

```rust
let dry = !raining;   // true becomes false, false becomes true
```

A small efficiency you get for free: SHORT-CIRCUITING. With &&, if the left side is already false, Rust does not even bother checking the right — the answer cannot change. With ||, a true on the left ends it early. This lets you write safe guards like:

```rust
if count > 0 && total / count > 5 { /* ... */ }
```

If count is 0, the left side is false, so Rust skips the division entirely — no divide-by-zero. The order of your conditions can protect you.

Comparisons (covered next) PRODUCE booleans, and these operators COMBINE them — together they express any real-world rule you can think of.

lessons.title: Comparison & Math Operators
lessons.body:
Operators are the verbs of arithmetic and logic. You have met most in passing — here they are, gathered in one place.

The math operators work as expected, with two worth a reminder:

```rust
10 + 3   // 13
10 - 3   // 7
10 * 3   // 30
10 / 3   // 3   — integer division drops the remainder
10 % 3   // 1   — remainder ("modulo")
```

COMPARISON operators ask a yes/no question and hand back a bool:

```rust
5 == 5   // true   — equal? (two equals signs!)
5 != 3   // true   — not equal
5 < 10   // true   — less than
5 > 10   // false  — greater than
5 <= 5   // true   — less than or equal
5 >= 6   // false  — greater than or equal
```

The classic trap: == compares, = assigns. Writing `if x = 5` is a mistake — and Rust rejects it, unlike some languages where it silently "works" and ruins your afternoon.

COMPOUND ASSIGNMENT updates a variable in place — read it as "and then store the result back":

```rust
let mut n = 10;
n += 5;   // n = n + 5  -> 15
n -= 2;   // 13
n *= 2;   // 26
n /= 3;   // 8  (integer division)
n %= 5;   // 3
```

These need a mut variable, since they change it. They are pure convenience: n += 5 is just shorter than n = n + 5, and Rustaceans use them constantly for counters and totals.

lessons.title: Reading User Input
lessons.body:
So far your programs only talk. Real tools also listen. Reading what someone types is a fundamental skill — and in Rust it has a small, fixed recipe worth memorizing.

First, bring in the input/output toolbox at the top of the file:

```rust
use std::io;
```

Then the four-step dance:

```rust
let mut name = String::new();          // 1. an empty box to fill

io::stdin()                            // 2. the keyboard
    .read_line(&mut name)              // 3. read a line INTO the box
    .expect("Failed to read line");    // 4. handle the rare failure

println!("Hello, {}", name.trim());
```

Reading it piece by piece:

• String::new() makes an empty, growable String — the box the typed text lands in.
• &mut name LENDS that box to read_line so it can write into it. It must be mut, because it is about to change.
• read_line can fail (imagine the keyboard unplugged mid-read), so it returns a Result. .expect("...") says "if it fails, crash with this message". You will learn gentler handling in the error-handling course — for now, .expect is fine.

One detail that trips up everyone: the typed text includes the ENTER key as a trailing newline. So always .trim() it before using — that strips the leftover newline and any stray spaces. Forget trim and your comparisons mysteriously never match.

lessons.title: Tuples & Destructuring
lessons.body:
A tuple is a way to bundle a FEW values of possibly DIFFERENT types into one. Think of it as a tiny, fixed-size package — perfect when values naturally travel together but do not deserve a whole named struct yet.

```rust
let point = (3, 7);                 // (i32, i32)
let person = ("Ada", 36, true);     // (&str, i32, bool) — mixed types!
```

You reach inside with a dot and a POSITION (zero-based):

```rust
let x = point.0;   // 3
let y = point.1;   // 7
```

But the elegant way to unpack a tuple is DESTRUCTURING — pulling all the pieces into named variables at once:

```rust
let (x, y) = point;            // x = 3, y = 7
let (name, age, member) = person;
```

One let, several names. This reads beautifully and is everywhere in Rust.

Tuples shine for returning MULTIPLE VALUES from a function:

```rust
fn min_max(v: &[i32]) -> (i32, i32) {
    // ... returns (smallest, largest)
}
let (lo, hi) = min_max(&data);   // unpack the pair
```

A couple of handy touches:
• Use `_` to IGNORE parts you do not need: `let (_, age, _) = person;`.
• The EMPTY tuple `()` is the "unit" type — it means "no meaningful value", and is what functions return when they have no `->`.
• Tuples have a fixed length and fixed types: you cannot push to one or change its shape. For a growing list of the SAME type, you want an array or a Vec (coming up).

The mental model: a tuple is an anonymous, fixed bundle. When the bundle gets important enough to deserve field names, graduate it to a struct. Until then, tuples and destructuring keep small groupings clean and readable.

lessons.title: Arrays & Slices
lessons.body:
An array is a FIXED-length row of values, all the SAME type, sitting together in memory. Fast and simple — but its size is locked in at compile time.

```rust
let days = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];        // [i32; 5]
let zeros = [0; 4];                 // [0, 0, 0, 0] — shorthand
let names = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"];
```

The type `[i32; 5]` literally means "5 i32s". That length is PART of the type — a [i32; 5] and a [i32; 6] are different types, and an array can never grow or shrink.

Access by index (zero-based), and Rust ALWAYS checks bounds:

```rust
let first = days[0];   // 1
let bad = days[99];    // PANICS — out of bounds, caught safely
```

That bounds check is a safety feature: other languages might hand you garbage memory, while Rust stops the program cleanly rather than reading where it should not.

Iterating is clean with a for loop:

```rust
for d in days {
    println!("{d}");
}
let total: i32 = days.iter().sum();
```

Now SLICES — a borrowed VIEW into part of an array (or Vec), without copying. A slice has type &[T]:

```rust
let middle = &days[1..4];   // a view of days[1], [2], [3]
```

The real power of slices is as FUNCTION PARAMETERS. Take &[T] and your function accepts arrays AND vectors AND sub-ranges — one signature, maximum flexibility:

```rust
fn sum(values: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    values.iter().sum()
}
sum(&days);            // works with an array
sum(&days[1..3]);      // works with a slice
```

The rule of thumb: use a fixed array when you know the exact count up front (a chessboard, RGB channels, days of the week); take &[T] in functions so they work with anything; and when you need a list that GROWS, reach for Vec — the very next lesson.

lessons.title: Formatting Output
lessons.body:
You know println! with {} placeholders. Inside those braces lives a small but powerful FORMATTING language that controls width, alignment, precision and number bases — the difference between messy output and a tidy table.

PRECISION for decimals (you have met this) — digits after the dot:

```rust
println!("{:.2}", 3.14159);   // 3.14
```

WIDTH pads a value to a minimum number of characters — great for aligning columns:

```rust
println!("{:5}", 42);    // "   42"  (right-aligned in 5 spaces)
println!("{:<5}", 42);   // "42   "  (left-aligned)
println!("{:^5}", 42);   // " 42  "  (centered)
```

The `<`, `>`, `^` choose left, right, center alignment. Combine padding with a fill character:

```rust
println!("{:0>5}", 42);  // "00042" — pad with zeros
println!("{:*^7}", "hi"); // "**hi***" — fill with *
```

NUMBER BASES let you print in binary, octal or hex — handy for bytes and flags:

```rust
println!("{:b}", 10);    // 1010   (binary)
println!("{:o}", 10);    // 12     (octal)
println!("{:x}", 255);   // ff     (hex, lowercase)
println!("{:#x}", 255);  // 0xff   (the # adds the 0x prefix)
```

You can mix these: width plus precision, named arguments, the debug `{:?}` and pretty-debug `{:#?}` (which prints structs across multiple indented lines — wonderful for inspecting nested data):

```rust
println!("{value:>8.2}", value = 3.14159);  // "    3.14"
println!("{:#?}", my_struct);                // multi-line debug
```

The takeaway: the format mini-language turns println! and format! into a precise output tool. You do not need to memorize it all — remember that `:.N` sets decimals, a number sets width, `<>^` align, and `:b/:o/:x` change base. Reach for `{:#?}` whenever you want to eyeball a complex value while debugging.

lessons.title: Reading Compiler Errors
lessons.body:
Here is a skill no one teaches but every Rustacean relies on: READING the compiler. Rust's error messages are famously helpful — often they tell you the exact fix. Learning to read them turns the "scary red wall" into a friendly guide.

A typical error has four parts:

```
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `s`
  --> src/main.rs:4:20
   |
2  |     let s = String::from("hi");
   |         - move occurs because `s` has type `String`...
3  |     let s2 = s;
   |              - value moved here
4  |     println!("{}", s);
   |                    ^ value borrowed here after move
   |
help: consider cloning the value
   |
3  |     let s2 = s.clone();
   |               ++++++++
```

Read it top to bottom:
1. The CODE (E0382) and a one-line summary — "borrow of moved value".
2. The LOCATION — file, line, column. Jump straight there.
3. The ANNOTATED source — arrows show where the problem is AND the related events (where the move happened).
4. Often a `help:` with a concrete suggested fix — here, add .clone().

Practical habits that make errors melt away:
• Fix the FIRST error first. One mistake often cascades into several; the later ones frequently vanish once you fix the first.
• READ the help line — Rust suggests the fix more often than not, sometimes with the exact characters to add.
• Look up the code: `rustc --explain E0382` prints a full explanation with examples.
• cargo check is your fast friend — it type-checks WITHOUT building a binary, so you get errors in a fraction of the time of a full build. Run it constantly.

For runtime debugging (not compile errors), two tools:
• The dbg! macro prints a value AND its line, then returns it — drop it anywhere: `let x = dbg!(a + b);`.
• A panic prints a message and a backtrace; set RUST_BACKTRACE=1 to see the call stack that led to it.

The mindset shift: the compiler is not rejecting you, it is PAIR-PROGRAMMING with you — catching mistakes now so they never reach your users. Slow down, read the message fully, and most errors fix themselves.

lessons.title: Ownership & Moves
lessons.body:
This is THE Rust idea — the one that makes it special. Take it slow.

Think of a value as a physical object, like a bicycle. A bicycle can't be in two garages at once: it has exactly ONE owner. Rust treats data the same way:

1. Every value has exactly one owner (a variable).
2. Only one owner at a time.
3. When the owner goes away, the value is thrown out automatically.

Watch what happens when you "assign" a String:

```rust
let s1 = String::from("hi");
let s2 = s1;          // the bicycle MOVES to s2
println!("{s1}");     // ❌ s1's garage is empty!
```

In Python this would copy a reference; in Rust the String MOVES. s1 isn't a second name for the data — it's an empty garage. The compiler stops you from using it. This is called a move.

Why so strict? Rule 3 is the payoff:

```rust
{
    let game = String::from("save data");
}   // <- game's owner is gone: memory freed
    //    HERE, instantly, automatically
```

No garbage collector pausing your game at random moments, no manual free() to forget — Rust always knows the exact moment data dies, because there is exactly one owner to watch.

Small print: simple fixed-size values (i32, bool, char) are so cheap to copy that Rust just copies them. let b = a; leaves both usable. Only heap data like String moves.

lessons.title: References & Borrowing
lessons.body:
Moving ownership everywhere would be exhausting — like GIVING someone your bicycle every time they want to look at it. The fix: lend it instead. That's borrowing, written with &:

```rust
fn measure(s: &String) -> usize {
    s.len()
}

let s = String::from("hello");
let n = measure(&s);  // lend, don't give
println!("{s}");      // ✅ still yours!
```

The & means "here, look at it, but I keep it". The function peeks at the value and hands it right back.

There are two kinds of lending:

```rust
let r = &s;      // read-only: "look at my notes"
let w = &mut s;  // editable:  "here's the pen"
```

And ONE law governs them, worth memorizing:

Any number of readers, OR exactly one writer — never both at once.

Why? Picture a shared document:
• 10 people reading at the same time? Fine — readers can't disturb each other.
• 2 people editing the same sentence simultaneously? Chaos.
• 1 editing while others read? They'd see half-finished sentences.

```rust
let r1 = &mut s;
let r2 = &mut s;  // ❌ two pens — refused!
```

Most languages let this chaos happen and you debug it at 2am. Rust's compiler simply refuses to compile it. That is what "fearless" means — and yes, fighting the borrow checker at first is normal. It is correcting habits other languages let slide.

lessons.title: Slices
lessons.body:
Sometimes you don't want to borrow the whole book — just chapter 3. A slice is exactly that: a borrowed VIEW into part of something, without copying anything.

```rust
let s = String::from("hello world");

let hello = &s[0..5];  // view of bytes 0-4
let world = &s[6..];   // from byte 6 to the end
```

Think of a slice as a bookmark plus a sticky note saying "from here to here". The text still lives in s — hello and world are just windows onto it. (Same end-excluded ranges as loops: 0..5 covers 0,1,2,3,4.)

Arrays slice the same way:

```rust
let scores = [10, 25, 40, 55, 70];
let middle = &scores[1..4]; // view of 25, 40, 55
```

Now the type you'll see everywhere: &str (say "string slice"). Surprise — every string literal is one:

```rust
let greeting = "hi there"; // type: &str
```

Literals are baked into your program, and "hi there" is just a view into that baked-in text.

Practical habit to steal: when a function only needs to READ text, take &str:

```rust
fn shout(text: &str) { /* ... */ }

shout("quick note");  // works with literals
shout(&my_string);    // works with Strings too
```

One parameter type, accepts both. That flexibility is why Rustaceans reach for &str by default.

lessons.title: The Stack & The Heap
lessons.body:
To really understand WHY ownership exists, peek at where your data physically lives. Programs use two kinds of memory, and they behave very differently.

The STACK is like a stack of plates. Fast, orderly, last-on first-off. Anything with a known fixed size goes here — an i32, a bool, a char. Pushing and popping is instant:

```rust
let x = 5;      // sits on the stack, size known: 4 bytes
let y = true;   // stack too
```

The HEAP is a big warehouse for things whose size is not known up front or might grow — like a String you keep typing into. You ask for space, the allocator finds a spot, and hands you back the ADDRESS. Slower, but flexible.

Here is the clever bit. A String is actually BOTH:

```rust
let s = String::from("hi");
```

On the stack sits a little 3-part ticket: a POINTER to the heap text, a LENGTH, and a CAPACITY. The actual characters "hi" live out in the heap warehouse.

Now the move rule suddenly makes sense:

```rust
let s2 = s;   // copies the 3-part TICKET, not the heap text
```

Both tickets would point at the SAME warehouse box. If both were valid, both would try to free that box when they end — a "double free" crash. So Rust invalidates s: one ticket, one owner, one cleanup. No bug possible.

And the Copy types from before? They are pure-stack values with no heap box behind them — so copying the whole thing is cheap and safe, no move needed. The stack/heap split IS the reason some types move and others copy.

lessons.title: Clone vs Copy
lessons.body:
You have bumped into both words already. Now let us pin down exactly how Copy and Clone differ — they sound similar but do very different work.

COPY is automatic and free-ish. Small, pure-stack types are marked Copy, so assigning them just duplicates the bytes and BOTH stay valid. No move, no ceremony:

```rust
let a = 5;
let b = a;        // a is copied
println!("{a} {b}");  // ✅ both fine — 5 5
```

Types that are Copy: integers, floats, bool, char, and tuples made only of those. The shared trait: they live entirely on the stack with a fixed size.

CLONE is explicit and possibly expensive. For heap-owning types like String or Vec, there is no free copy — duplicating them means allocating a whole new heap box and copying the contents. Rust refuses to do that silently; you must ASK with .clone():

```rust
let s1 = String::from("hi");
let s2 = s1.clone();   // brand-new heap box, real duplicate
println!("{s1} {s2}"); // ✅ both own their own data
```

The design principle is honesty about cost: cheap copies happen automatically, expensive ones must be requested in plain sight. When you see .clone(), you know a real allocation may be happening — a useful signal when hunting for slow code.

For your own structs, you opt in with a one-line annotation:

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]   // now this type copies like an integer
struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }
```

A struct can only be Copy if every field is Copy — put a String inside and Copy is off the table, but Clone is still available.

lessons.title: Lifetimes Basics
lessons.body:
Lifetimes look scary — those little 'a tags — but the idea is gentle: a reference must never outlive the data it points to. Lifetimes are just labels that let the compiler check that.

Recall the danger. A reference is a borrowed ticket to someone else's data. If the data is freed but you still hold the ticket, you have a DANGLING reference — pointing at memory that is gone. C lets this happen; Rust does not:

```rust
fn dangle() -> &String {       // ❌ won't compile
    let s = String::from("hi");
    &s        // s dies at the brace — this ticket would dangle
}
```

s is dropped when the function ends, so returning a reference to it would hand back a ticket to freed memory. Rust catches this at compile time.

Most of the time lifetimes are INVISIBLE — the compiler infers them. You only write them when a function returns a reference and Rust cannot tell which input it came from:

```rust
fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if x.len() > y.len() { x } else { y }
}
```

Read 'a as a label: "the returned reference lives as long as BOTH inputs". You are not changing how long anything lives — you are PROMISING a relationship, and the compiler holds you to it.

The key mindset shifts:

• Lifetimes describe relationships, they do not extend anything.
• You meet them mostly in error messages, not by writing them.
• When the compiler asks for one, it is preventing a real dangling-pointer bug.

lessons.title: Taming the Borrow Checker
lessons.body:
Everyone fights the borrow checker at first. The secret: its complaints fall into a few patterns, each with a standard fix. Learn the patterns and the fights end.

PATTERN 1 — "use of moved value". You used something after giving it away.

```rust
let s = String::from("hi");
let s2 = s;
println!("{s}");   // ❌ s was moved into s2
```
Fix: borrow instead (let s2 = &s;), or clone if you truly need two (let s2 = s.clone();).

PATTERN 2 — "cannot borrow as mutable more than once". Two &mut at the same time.

```rust
let r1 = &mut v;
let r2 = &mut v;   // ❌
```
Fix: finish using r1 before creating r2 — remember borrows end at last use.

PATTERN 3 — "cannot borrow as mutable because also borrowed as immutable". A reader and a writer overlap.

```rust
let first = &v[0];
v.push(10);        // ❌ push needs &mut while first (a &) is alive
println!("{first}");
```
Fix: reorder so the reader is done before the writer starts, or clone the value you read out.

PATTERN 4 — "returns a reference to data owned by the current function" (dangling).
Fix: return the owned value instead of a reference.

The universal strategies: (1) shrink how long a borrow lives by using it sooner, (2) reorder reads before writes, (3) clone as a deliberate escape hatch when sharing is genuinely needed, and (4) READ the compiler message — Rust's errors literally suggest the fix more often than not. The borrow checker is not your enemy; it is a very pedantic colleague catching real bugs.

lessons.title: Deriving Common Traits
lessons.body:
Your fresh struct cannot be printed, copied, or compared — Rust gives it no behavior for free. But writing that boilerplate by hand is tedious, so Rust can GENERATE it with one line: `#[derive(...)]`.

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }
```

That single attribute writes three implementations for you. The most useful derivable traits:

• Debug — enables `{:?}` printing, the developer's view. Without it, `println!("{p:?}")` will not compile.

```rust
let p = Point { x: 1, y: 2 };
println!("{p:?}");   // Point { x: 1, y: 2 }
```

• Clone — adds `.clone()` for an explicit deep copy.
• Copy — makes the struct copy-on-assign like an integer (only if every field is Copy).
• PartialEq / Eq — enable `==` and `!=` between instances.
• PartialOrd / Ord — enable the comparison operators `<` and `>` (Ord also unlocks sorting; PartialOrd alone just gives the operators).
• Default — adds `Type::default()` giving zero/empty values.
• Hash — lets the struct be a HashMap key or HashSet member.

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
struct Color { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 }

let a = Color { r: 255, g: 0, b: 0 };
let b = a;            // Copy: a still usable
println!("{}", a == b);  // PartialEq: true
```

The rule: derive what you need, and remember a derive only works if all FIELDS support it (you cannot derive Copy on a struct containing a String). For custom behavior — say a fancy Display format — you implement the trait by hand instead. But for the everyday traits, `#[derive]` saves you pages of boilerplate.

lessons.title: Enums as State Machines
lessons.body:
Enums in Rust are far more powerful than a list of names — each variant can CARRY DATA. This turns them into the perfect tool for modeling states, and "making illegal states unrepresentable".

```rust
enum Shape {
    Circle(f64),              // radius
    Rectangle(f64, f64),      // width, height
    Triangle { base: f64, height: f64 },  // named fields too
}
```

One Shape value is EXACTLY one of these, with exactly the data that variant needs. A circle simply has no width field to misuse. Compare that to a struct with optional width/height/radius all nullable — a swamp of invalid combinations. The enum makes the swamp impossible.

You handle them with match, destructuring the data out of each variant:

```rust
fn area(s: &Shape) -> f64 {
    match s {
        Shape::Circle(r) => 3.14159 * r * r,
        Shape::Rectangle(w, h) => w * h,
        Shape::Triangle { base, height } => 0.5 * base * height,
    }
}
```

This shines for STATE MACHINES — modeling something that moves between distinct states, each carrying its own data:

```rust
enum Connection {
    Disconnected,
    Connecting { attempt: u32 },
    Connected { session_id: String },
}
```

A connection is in ONE state at a time, and the data it carries depends on the state — a session_id exists only when Connected. Transition functions take a state and return the next, and because match is exhaustive, the compiler guarantees you handled every state. Forget one and it will not compile.

The big idea: model your domain with enums so that invalid states cannot even be written. The compiler then enforces your logic for you — fewer bugs, by construction.

lessons.title: Strings in Depth
lessons.body:
You already know the cast: String is the owned, growable whiteboard; &str is a read-only photo of text. Now the daily verbs:

```rust
let mut s = String::from("Hello");
s.push_str(", world");      // append a &str
s.push('!');                // append ONE char

let name = "Ferris";
let msg = format!("Hi {name}, you have {} coins", 42);
```

format! is println!'s twin that hands you the String instead of printing it — the workhorse for building text.

Now the famous surprise: `s[0]` does NOT compile. Why? Rust strings are UTF-8, where characters have different byte sizes:

```rust
let crab = "🦀";
println!("{}", crab.len());           // 4 (bytes!)
println!("{}", crab.chars().count()); // 1 (character)
```

"h" is 1 byte, "é" is 2, "🦀" is 4. So "give me character 0" is genuinely ambiguous — byte 0? char 0? Rust makes you say which:

```rust
for c in "héllo".chars() {   // by character
    print!("[{c}]");
}
let bytes = s.as_bytes();    // by byte
```

This feels pedantic until the day your app meets real names, emoji, and non-English text — and just works while other apps garble them. Common conversions to memorize: `"x".to_string()` and `String::from("x")` go &str → String; `&s` goes String → &str.

lessons.title: HashSet & Uniqueness
lessons.body:
A Vec keeps everything, duplicates and all. But often you want a collection of UNIQUE things, with instant "is this in here?" checks. That is a HashSet.

```rust
use std::collections::HashSet;

let mut seen = HashSet::new();
seen.insert("apple");
seen.insert("apple");   // ignored — already present
seen.insert("banana");

println!("{}", seen.len());          // 2, not 3
println!("{}", seen.contains("apple"));  // true
```

The two superpowers:

• Automatic deduplication — inserting a value already present does nothing. insert returns a bool: true if newly added, false if it was already there.
• O(1) membership — contains() is near-instant regardless of size, unlike scanning a Vec which gets slower as it grows.

A common one-liner: dedupe a Vec by funneling it through a set.

```rust
let nums = vec![1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3];
let unique: HashSet<_> = nums.into_iter().collect();
```

HashSets also do SET ALGEBRA, reading just like math:

```rust
let a: HashSet<i32> = [1, 2, 3].into_iter().collect();
let b: HashSet<i32> = [2, 3, 4].into_iter().collect();

a.intersection(&b);  // {2, 3} — in both
a.union(&b);         // {1, 2, 3, 4} — in either
a.difference(&b);    // {1} — in a but not b
```

Like HashMap keys, the elements must be Hashable and comparable (most built-in types are; derive Hash + Eq for your own). And like a HashMap, order is NOT preserved — if you need sorted unique values, reach for BTreeSet instead. Use HashSet whenever the question is "have I seen this?" or "what are the distinct values?".

lessons.title: Iterating & Collecting
lessons.body:
Collections become truly powerful when you stop writing manual loops and start TRANSFORMING them with iterators. The pattern is always the same three beats: get an iterator, chain adapters, collect the result.

```rust
let nums = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];

let result: Vec<i32> = nums.iter()
    .filter(|&&n| n % 2 == 0)   // keep evens
    .map(|&n| n * 10)           // transform each
    .collect();                 // gather into a Vec
// result = [20, 40, 60]
```

The key players:
• .iter() — borrow each element; .into_iter() — take ownership; .iter_mut() — borrow mutably.
• ADAPTERS like map, filter, take, skip, enumerate — each returns a new lazy iterator. Nothing actually runs until you consume it.
• CONSUMERS like collect, sum, count, for_each — these trigger the work and produce a final value.

`collect` is the shape-shifter: it can build many collection types, and you tell it which via the target type:

```rust
let v: Vec<i32> = (1..=3).collect();              // a Vec
let s: HashSet<i32> = vec![1, 1, 2].into_iter().collect();  // a Set
let m: HashMap<_, _> = vec![("a", 1)].into_iter().collect(); // a Map
```

A lovely trick: collecting an iterator of Results into a Result<Vec<_>, _> — it short-circuits, giving Ok(all values) or the first Err. And `enumerate` pairs each item with its index:

```rust
for (i, item) in list.iter().enumerate() {
    println!("{i}: {item}");
}
```

The mindset shift: describe WHAT you want (filter these, transform those, gather here) rather than HOW to loop. The code reads like a sentence, and the compiler often makes it as fast as a hand-written loop — zero-cost abstraction at work.

lessons.title: Nested & Combined Collections
lessons.body:
Real programs rarely use a single flat collection. They combine them: a list of structs, a map of lists, a map of maps. Composing collections is how you model real data — and Rust's types make the shape explicit.

A VEC OF STRUCTS — the everyday "table of records":

```rust
struct Player { name: String, score: u32 }

let mut players = vec![
    Player { name: "Ada".into(), score: 90 },
    Player { name: "Linus".into(), score: 85 },
];
players.sort_by(|a, b| b.score.cmp(&a.score)); // sort by score desc
```

A MAP OF VECS — grouping (one key, many values):

```rust
let mut teams: HashMap<String, Vec<String>> = HashMap::new();
teams.entry("red".into()).or_default().push("Ada".into());
```

A MAP OF MAPS — two-level lookup, like settings.section.key:

```rust
let mut config: HashMap<String, HashMap<String, String>> = HashMap::new();
```

The type signature is your friend here: HashMap<String, Vec<Player>> reads top to bottom as exactly its structure — a map from a String to a list of Players. When a type looks scary, read it outside-in and it explains itself.

Two practical tips:
• Reach for type aliases when nesting gets deep — `type Grid = Vec<Vec<u8>>;` makes signatures readable.
• Accessing deep into nests, prefer .get() which returns Option, over indexing which can panic. Chain with `?` or and_then to walk levels safely.

```rust
let cell = grid.get(row).and_then(|r| r.get(col)); // Option<&u8>, no panic
```

The skill is COMPOSITION: pick the right container at each level (Vec for ordered lists, HashMap for keyed lookup, HashSet for uniqueness) and nest them to match your data. Almost any real-world structure is just these few collections combined.

lessons.title: Iterators
lessons.body:
You've looped with for. Iterators are the same idea as an assembly line: a source, transformation stations, and a collector at the end:

```rust
let v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];

let result: Vec<i32> = v.iter()      // source
    .filter(|x| *x % 2 == 0)         // keep evens
    .map(|x| x * 2)                  // double them
    .collect();                      // box them up
// [4, 8, 12]
```

Read it like a sentence: "from v, keep the evens, double each, collect into a Vec." Each station takes a closure — last lesson's verbs at work.

The crucial mental model: iterators are LAZY. filter and map do nothing on their own — they just describe the line. Work happens only when a consumer asks for results:

```rust
v.iter().map(|x| x * 2);          // nothing ran!
let n: i32 = v.iter().sum();      // sum DRIVES the line
let big = v.iter().max();         // Option<&i32>
let evens = v.iter()
    .filter(|x| *x % 2 == 0)
    .count();                     // 3
```

Like a sushi conveyor: plates only get made when someone takes them.

Why prefer this over hand-rolled loops? It reads as WHAT you want, not HOW; the closures keep logic in one place; chains compile down to the same speed as manual loops (zero-cost again); and — quietly profound — your for loops were iterators all along: `for x in &v` calls into the same machinery.

Daily five to memorize: map, filter, sum, count, collect. They cover 90% of real pipelines.

lessons.title: Box & the Heap
lessons.body:
Quick memory tour. Your program has two storage areas:

• The STACK — a neat pile of fixed-size boxes. Blazing fast, but everything's size must be known up front.
• The HEAP — a giant warehouse. Any size, any time, slightly slower to reach.

Box<T> is a claim ticket: the value goes to the warehouse, and the small ticket (a pointer) sits on the stack:

```rust
let b = Box::new(5);       // 5 lives in the warehouse
println!("{}", *b + 1);    // * follows the ticket: 6
```

The ticket follows normal ownership — when the Box is dropped, the warehouse slot is freed. Automatically. (You already knew that rule; Box just extends it to the heap.)

"Why would I box a tiny 5?" You wouldn't. Box earns its keep in three real situations:

1. Recursive types — the puzzle that NEEDS it. Try a type containing itself:

```rust
enum Train {
    Car(u32, Train),   // ❌ infinite size!
    Caboose,
}
```

How big is a Train? A u32 plus a Train, which is a u32 plus a Train, which is… the compiler cannot allocate infinity. The fix: store a TICKET instead of the train itself —

```rust
enum Train {
    Car(u32, Box<Train>),  // ✅ ticket = known size
    Caboose,
}
```

2. Huge data you move around — moving a Box moves the small ticket, not the cargo.

3. Trait objects — Box<dyn Speak> from the traits project: "a ticket to SOMETHING that can speak", exact type decided at runtime.

lessons.title: Rc & RefCell
lessons.body:
Ownership rule #1: one owner per value. It's served you well — but sometimes reality disagrees. A song belongs to THREE playlists. A game item sits in the inventory AND the quick-bar. Who's the owner?

Rc<T> (Reference Counted) makes shared ownership legal. Think of it as a shared Netflix account that tracks how many people use it:

```rust
use std::rc::Rc;

let song = Rc::new(String::from("Crab Rave"));

let playlist_a = Rc::clone(&song); // +1 user
let playlist_b = Rc::clone(&song); // +1 user

println!("{}", Rc::strong_count(&song)); // 3
```

Key insight: Rc::clone does NOT copy the song — it just bumps the user counter and hands out another handle. When the last handle drops, the count hits zero and the data is freed. Ownership rules, upgraded from "one owner" to "the count knows".

The catch: Rc handles are READ-ONLY (many owners + mutation = the chaos the borrow checker exists to prevent). When shared data must also change, RefCell<T> joins:

```rust
use std::cell::RefCell;

let score = Rc::new(RefCell::new(0));
let handle = Rc::clone(&score);

*handle.borrow_mut() += 10;   // checked at RUNTIME
println!("{}", score.borrow()); // 10
```

RefCell moves the borrow rules from compile time to runtime: break them (two borrow_mut() alive at once) and it panics instead of failing to compile. A sharper tool — same laws, later enforcement.

Two fine-print warnings: Rc is single-threaded only (its thread-safe sibling Arc appears in the concurrency course), and reference CYCLES (A points to B points to A) can leak — Weak<T> exists for breaking them.

lessons.title: Iterator Adapters in Depth
lessons.body:
Iterator adapters are LEGO bricks. Each takes an iterator and returns a new one, so you snap them together into a pipeline that reads like a description of the result. Beyond map and filter, a handful of adapters cover almost everything.

```rust
let nums = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];

let result: Vec<i32> = nums.iter()
    .skip(1)             // drop the first: 2,3,4,5,6
    .take(3)             // keep next three: 2,3,4
    .map(|n| n * 10)     // 20,30,40
    .collect();
```

The essential adapters:
• map — transform each element.
• filter — keep elements passing a test.
• take(n) / skip(n) — keep the first n / drop the first n.
• take_while / skip_while — by a condition instead of a count.
• enumerate — pair each item with its index.
• zip — walk two iterators in lockstep, pairing their items.
• chain — glue two iterators end to end.
• flatten / flat_map — collapse nested iterators into one stream.
• rev — reverse (on iterators that support it).

Two that combine beautifully — zip and map:

```rust
let names = ["Ada", "Bo"];
let ages = [37, 9];
let pairs: Vec<String> = names.iter()
    .zip(ages.iter())                  // ("Ada",37), ("Bo",9)
    .map(|(n, a)| format!("{n} is {a}"))
    .collect();
```

The golden rule again: adapters are LAZY. The whole chain does nothing until a CONSUMER (collect, sum, count, for_each, find) pulls values through it. So a million-element chain with a `.find()` stops the instant it hits a match — it never processes the rest.

This style is not just pretty; it is FAST. The compiler fuses the whole pipeline into a single tight loop with no intermediate collections — the same speed as a hand-rolled loop, but reading like a sentence. Master these bricks and most "loop and accumulate" code becomes one clear, efficient chain.

lessons.title: Closure Traits: Fn, FnMut, FnOnce
lessons.body:
A closure is a function that can CAPTURE variables from its surroundings. How it captures them determines which of three traits it implements — and that controls how many times it can be called and what it can do.

The three traits, from most to least restrictive on the closure (most to least permissive on the caller):

• FnOnce — can be called AT LEAST once; may CONSUME (move) its captures. Every closure is at least FnOnce.
• FnMut — can be called multiple times and may MUTATE its captures.
• Fn — can be called multiple times and only READS its captures (or captures nothing).

The compiler picks the most permissive trait a closure qualifies for, based on what it does with its captures:

```rust
let x = 10;
let read = || println!("{x}");      // only reads x -> Fn

let mut count = 0;
let mut tick = || count += 1;       // mutates count -> FnMut

let s = String::from("hi");
let consume = move || drop(s);      // moves s away -> FnOnce
```

When you WRITE a function that accepts a closure, you choose the bound:

```rust
fn call_twice<F: Fn()>(f: F) { f(); f(); }      // needs callable 2+ times, read-only
fn run_once<F: FnOnce()>(f: F) { f(); }          // called once, most flexible
```

`FnOnce` as a parameter bound is the most ACCEPTING — it takes any closure, because every closure is FnOnce. `Fn` is the most DEMANDING — it only accepts read-only ones. So: bound your parameter as loosely as your function actually needs (FnOnce if you call once), to accept the widest range of closures.

The `move` keyword forces a closure to TAKE OWNERSHIP of its captures rather than borrow them. It is essential when a closure outlives the current scope — handing it to a thread, returning it, or storing it — because the captured data must travel WITH the closure.

lessons.title: Option & Result Combinators
lessons.body:
Reaching for match on every Option and Result gets verbose fast. COMBINATORS are methods that transform these types in one fluent step — the same functional style as iterator adapters, applied to "maybe a value" and "value or error".

On OPTION:
• map — transform the inner value if it is Some, leave None alone.
• and_then — like map, but the closure itself returns an Option (chaining fallible steps).
• unwrap_or(default) — the value, or a fallback if None.
• unwrap_or_else(|| ...) — fallback computed lazily.
• filter — keep Some only if a predicate holds.

```rust
let len = Some("hello")
    .map(|s| s.len())        // Some(5)
    .filter(|&n| n > 3)      // still Some(5)
    .unwrap_or(0);           // 5
```

On RESULT:
• map — transform the Ok value.
• map_err — transform the Err value (great for converting error types).
• and_then — chain another operation that returns a Result.
• unwrap_or / ok() — provide a default, or turn a Result into an Option.

```rust
let n: i32 = "42".parse::<i32>()
    .map(|x| x * 2)          // Ok(84)
    .unwrap_or(-1);          // 84, or -1 if parse failed
```

The key distinction, worth memorizing:
• map when your closure returns a PLAIN value → keeps the same wrapper.
• and_then when your closure returns ANOTHER Option/Result → flattens, so you do not end up with Option<Option<T>>.

```rust
fn first_char(s: &str) -> Option<char> { s.chars().next() }

let c = Some("hi").and_then(first_char);  // Some('h'), not Some(Some('h'))
```

The payoff: long if-let/match ladders collapse into readable chains, and the "happy path" reads top to bottom while None/Err cases are handled gracefully without ever panicking. This combinator style is everywhere in idiomatic Rust.

lessons.title: Folding & Reducing
lessons.body:
Many computations boil a whole collection down to ONE value: a sum, a product, a maximum, a built-up string. The general tool for this is fold — the Swiss-army knife behind sum(), product(), count() and more.

fold takes an INITIAL accumulator and a closure that combines the accumulator with each element:

```rust
let nums = [1, 2, 3, 4];
let sum = nums.iter().fold(0, |acc, &x| acc + x);   // 10
```

Read it as: start the accumulator at 0; for each x, replace acc with acc + x. After the last element, acc is the answer. The same shape computes very different things just by changing the seed and the closure:

```rust
let product = nums.iter().fold(1, |acc, &x| acc * x);     // 24 (seed 1!)
let max = nums.iter().fold(i32::MIN, |a, &x| a.max(x));   // 4
let csv = nums.iter().fold(String::new(),
    |mut s, &x| { if !s.is_empty() { s.push(','); } s.push_str(&x.to_string()); s });
```

Notice the accumulator can be ANY type — a number, a String, even a HashMap — which makes fold able to build up rich results, not just sum numbers.

A close cousin is reduce, which uses the FIRST element as the seed (so it returns an Option, since an empty iterator has no first element):

```rust
let max = nums.iter().copied().reduce(|a, b| a.max(b));   // Some(4)
```

Use reduce when a separate seed makes no sense (like max/min of a non-empty list); use fold when you need a distinct starting value or a different accumulator type.

The mental model: fold is "carry a running result through the collection, updating it at each step". Once you see that pattern, you will recognize that sum, count, max, joining strings, and tallying into a map are all the SAME operation with different seeds and combiners. It is one of the most powerful ideas in functional programming.

lessons.title: Unsafe Rust
lessons.body:
Sometimes you must tell the compiler: "step aside — I'll vouch for this part personally." That's the unsafe block. Despite the scary name, it does NOT turn off Rust's rules. It unlocks exactly five extra abilities (the "five superpowers"), the big two being: dereference raw pointers, and call functions marked unsafe.

```rust
let x = 5;
let p = &x as *const i32;  // raw pointer: fine to MAKE

unsafe {
    println!("{}", *p);    // following it needs the block
}
```

Everything else — ownership, types, bounds on normal references — stays fully enforced inside the block. unsafe isn't "anything goes"; it's a highlighted region saying "the compiler can't verify THIS bit, a human did."

Why does it exist at all? Three honest reasons:

• Talking to hardware — the embedded course's registers are raw memory addresses.
• Talking to C — calling into existing C libraries (FFI) is inherently unverifiable.
• Building safe abstractions — here's the open secret: Vec, String, Rc… contain unsafe internally! Their authors verified the tricky pointer work once, wrapped it in a safe API, and millions use it without ever touching unsafe.

That last point is the culture, and it matters more than the syntax:

1. Reach for safe Rust first — it almost always suffices.
2. If you truly need unsafe, keep the block TINY.
3. Wrap it in a safe function that makes misuse impossible.
4. Comment the invariant — WHY is this sound?

Most Rust developers write unsafe a handful of times a year. Knowing how to read it — and respect it — is the real skill.

options: Skipping the borrow checker because it is annoying
Talking to hardware registers or C libraries

lessons.title: Mutex: Shared Mutable State
lessons.body:
Channels let threads communicate by SENDING data. But sometimes several threads need to SHARE and modify the same data — a counter, a cache, a game world. For that you need a Mutex: a lock that guarantees only one thread touches the data at a time.

Mutex stands for "MUTual EXclusion". Picture a single key to a room: to use what is inside, a thread must grab the key (LOCK), do its work, then return the key (UNLOCK). While one thread holds the key, others wait.

```rust
use std::sync::Mutex;

let counter = Mutex::new(0);

{
    let mut num = counter.lock().unwrap();  // acquire the lock
    *num += 1;                              // safely mutate
}   // lock released automatically at end of scope
```

Two things make Rust's Mutex special and safe:

1. The data lives INSIDE the Mutex. You cannot access it without locking — the type system makes forgetting to lock impossible. Contrast with other languages where the lock and the data are separate, and forgetting to lock is a silent bug.

2. The lock auto-releases via Drop when the guard goes out of scope. No manual unlock to forget, even if a panic occurs.

lock() returns a Result (it errors only if another thread panicked while holding the lock — a "poisoned" mutex), and a guard that derefs to the inner data with `*`.

The classic danger Mutex introduces is DEADLOCK: thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2, while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1 — both stuck forever. Avoid it by always acquiring multiple locks in a CONSISTENT order, and holding locks for as short a time as possible.

A Mutex alone is not shareable across threads, though — you need to wrap it so multiple threads can co-own it. That wrapper is Arc, the very next lesson. Mutex makes mutation safe; Arc makes sharing possible; together they are how Rust shares mutable state without data races.

lessons.title: Send & Sync
lessons.body:
How does Rust KNOW that Arc is safe to share across threads but Rc is not? Two marker traits encode the rules of thread safety: Send and Sync. They are the quiet guardians behind Rust's "fearless concurrency".

SEND — a type is Send if it can be safely MOVED to another thread. Most types are: i32, String, Vec. A type is NOT Send if moving it across threads would be unsafe (Rc, because its non-atomic count could be corrupted by two threads).

SYNC — a type is Sync if it can be safely SHARED by reference (&T) between threads. Equivalently, &T is Send. A Mutex<T> is Sync (that is its whole job); a Cell/RefCell is not Sync (their interior mutability is not thread-safe).

These traits are MARKERS — they have no methods. They simply tag a type as "thread-safe in this way", and the compiler derives them AUTOMATICALLY: a struct is Send if all its fields are Send, Sync if all its fields are Sync. You almost never implement them by hand.

The payoff is enormous. When you write `thread::spawn(move || ...)`, the closure's captured data is required to be Send. So if you try to capture an Rc:

```rust
let data = Rc::new(5);
thread::spawn(move || println!("{data}"));  // ❌ Rc is not Send
```

…the compiler stops you at COMPILE TIME with a clear message. The entire category of "I accidentally shared something thread-unsafe" becomes impossible. Swap Rc for Arc (which IS Send + Sync) and it compiles.

This is the secret of fearless concurrency: data-race safety is not a runtime hope or a code-review checklist — it is a TYPE-LEVEL guarantee. The same ownership and borrowing rules that prevent memory bugs, extended with Send and Sync, prevent data races too. You write concurrent code and the compiler simply will not let the unsafe versions compile.

lessons.title: Why Rust for ML & Working with Data
lessons.body:
Normal programming: you write the rules. "IF email contains 'WIN MONEY' THEN spam." Machine learning flips it: you show the computer thousands of examples — spam and not-spam — and it figures out the rules itself. Teaching by example instead of instruction.

Why do this in Rust? Python is where ML research happens, but shipping models to real users is a different job — and there Rust shines: one small fast binary, no random garbage-collector pauses mid-request.

Your Python-to-Rust dictionary:

• NumPy → ndarray (grids of numbers)
• scikit-learn → linfa (classic ML toolkit)
• PyTorch → Burn (deep learning)
• running LLMs → Candle (tiny and fast, by Hugging Face)

Underneath all of it, ML is just arithmetic on lists of numbers — which you already know how to do:

```rust
let temps = [22.1, 23.4, 21.8, 24.0];

let mean: f64 = temps.iter().sum::<f64>()
              / temps.len() as f64;
```

One habit to learn immediately: NORMALIZE your data. Imagine comparing people by height-in-millimeters (1700!) and shoe-size (42). The huge numbers shout, the small ones whisper, and the model only hears shouting. The fix puts everything on one scale:

```rust
let normalized = (x - mean) / std;
```

Subtract the average, divide by the spread. Now "unusually large" looks the same whether it started as millimeters or shoe sizes. Models learn dramatically better this way — and that formula is your first project, one screen from now.

lessons.title: Linear Regression from Scratch
lessons.body:
Plot some house sales on paper: size across, price up. The dots roughly form a line — bigger house, higher price. If you could DRAW the best line through those dots, you could predict the price of any house. That's linear regression, the Hello World of ML.

A line is just two numbers:

```rust
prediction = w * x + b
```

• w (weight) — the slope: "every extra m² adds this much price"
• b (bias) — where the line starts when x is 0

Training means finding good values for w and b. But how do you know if a line is good? Measure how wrong it is — that score is called the loss:

```rust
error = prediction - actual_price
loss  = average of error * error
```

Perfect line: loss near 0. Terrible line: huge loss.

Now the magic trick that powers ALL of modern AI, including ChatGPT — gradient descent. Imagine standing on a foggy hillside where altitude = loss. You can't see the valley, but you can feel which way is downhill. So: take a small step down. Repeat 1000 times.

```rust
let pred = w * x + b;
let error = pred - y;
w -= lr * error * x;   // step downhill
b -= lr * error;
```

lr is the learning rate — your step size, and it's a Goldilocks number:
• Too small (0.0000001) — you'll reach the valley next year.
• Too big (10.0) — you LEAP over the valley and land higher than you started. Loss explodes.
• Just right — the loss shrinks every round, and you watch the model literally learn.

You'll see exactly that in this lesson's project: a house-price model whose loss melts away as it trains.

lessons.title: Classification with k-NN
lessons.body:
Last lesson predicted a NUMBER (a price). Just as often you need to predict a CATEGORY: spam or not? cat or dog? ripe or unripe? That's classification.

Meet the friendliest classifier ever invented: k-Nearest Neighbors. The whole idea fits in one sentence:

"You're probably similar to whatever is closest to you."

A new kid joins school and you know nothing about them — but the three kids they always stand with are all basketball players. Your guess? Basketball player. That's the entire algorithm:

1. Measure the distance from the mystery point to every example you've seen.
2. Grab the k closest ones (k = 3, say).
3. Let them vote. Majority wins.

"Distance" is real geometric distance. Plot fruit by (weight, sweetness) and similar fruits land near each other. Straight-line distance is just Pythagoras:

```rust
fn dist(a: (f64, f64), b: (f64, f64)) -> f64 {
    ((a.0 - b.0).powi(2)
   + (a.1 - b.1).powi(2)).sqrt()
}
```

Square the difference in each direction, add, square-root. Middle-school math, now a classifier.

Why k instead of just the single nearest? One mislabeled example right next to your mystery point would fool you. With k = 7, that one weirdo gets outvoted by six sensible neighbors. Small k = jumpy; big k = smooth but blurry. Picking k is your first taste of "tuning" a model.

(In production you'd grab linfa's ready-made version — but after building it yourself in the project, it will never be a black box.)

questions.explanation: "Tell me who your neighbors are and I'll tell you who you are" — the k nearest known examples vote on the answer.

questions.prompt: Euclidean distance between two 2D points is…

lessons.title: Deep Learning with Burn & Candle
lessons.body:
In the perceptron lesson, you computed weight updates BY HAND. Respect earned — now meet the machinery that does it at scale.

First word: tensor. Sounds exotic, means "n-dimensional array of numbers". A number is a 0-d tensor, your temps list 1-d, a grayscale image 2-d, a batch of color images 4-d. Deep learning is tensor arithmetic, performed billions of times — which is why frameworks exist to make it fast and automatic.

Second word — the big one: autodiff (automatic differentiation). In linear regression YOU derived the gradient (that `error * x` term). Autodiff frameworks watch every operation in the forward pass and derive ALL gradients automatically. A million-parameter network trains with the same three lines as your perceptron — the framework does calculus so you do architecture.

The two Rust players:

• Burn — the full training framework (think PyTorch). Its signature move is swappable backends: the SAME model code runs on NdArray (pure CPU), WGPU (any GPU — graphics API, works everywhere), or LibTorch. Write once, train anywhere.

```rust
// Burn flavor (simplified)
let model = Linear::new(2, 1);
let out = model.forward(input);
let grads = loss.backward(); // autodiff!
```

• Candle — Hugging Face's minimalist inference engine. Skips training entirely; obsesses over running models small and fast. No 800MB runtime — Candle binaries are tiny and boot instantly, which makes LLMs on serverless (Lambda, Workers) actually practical.

The decision rule: training or research → Burn. Shipping inference, especially LLMs → Candle. Either way, the tensor ops underneath are exactly what you build in this project.

lessons.body:
Final ML lesson: what actually happens when you chat with an AI — and where Rust fits in each step of the pipeline.

Step 1: Tokenization. Models don't read letters; they read token IDs — numbered puzzle pieces. "unbelievable" might split into "un" + "believ" + "able", each with an ID. Fun fact with a punchline: Hugging Face's tokenizers library — the one the entire Python ML world calls — is written in Rust. Python AI has been running Rust all along.

Step 2: The forward pass. Token IDs flow through the network (those matvec operations you just wrote, times billions) and out comes a probability for every possible next token.

Step 3: Sampling. Pick from those probabilities. The temperature knob you've seen in AI apps lives here: low = always take the safest token (predictable), high = gamble on unlikely ones (creative, chaotic). Then append the chosen token and repeat — LLMs generate one token at a time, in a loop.

Making this practical on your own hardware: quantization — storing weights in 4-8 bits instead of 32. A model that needed a data-center GPU shrinks onto a laptop, trading a sliver of quality. That's what those GGUF files are; Candle loads them.

Step 4: Serving. Wrap it in an HTTP API — axum (built on tokio, your async lesson) is the standard Rust choice. Tokenizer + Candle + axum = a chat endpoint, one small binary, no Python anywhere.

One more concept earns a mention: embeddings — vectors that capture MEANING, where similar texts get nearby vectors (your k-NN distance skills, applied to semantics). They power search and retrieval (RAG) in serious AI apps.

lessons.title: Gradient Descent Step by Step
lessons.body:
Almost every model "learns" the same way: gradient descent. Strip away the math and it is just walking downhill in the dark.

Imagine you are blindfolded on a hill and want the lowest point. You feel the slope under your feet and take a small step DOWNHILL. Repeat. Eventually you reach the bottom. That bottom is the model with the least error.

The pieces:

• LOSS — a single number measuring how wrong the model is. Lower is better. We want to minimize it.
• GRADIENT — the slope of the loss with respect to each parameter: "which way is uphill, and how steep?"
• LEARNING RATE — how big a step to take. Too big and you overshoot the valley; too small and you crawl forever.

The update rule, in plain code:

```rust
// one parameter `w`, learning rate `lr`
let gradient = compute_gradient(&data, w);
w = w - lr * gradient;   // step DOWNHILL (opposite the slope)
```

Run that thousands of times and w drifts toward the value that minimizes loss. That subtraction is the whole idea: move AGAINST the gradient, scaled by the learning rate.

Two everyday troubles:

• Learning rate too HIGH → loss bounces around or explodes to NaN. Lower it (try 0.01, 0.001).
• Learning rate too LOW → training is painfully slow. Nudge it up.

This single loop — predict, measure loss, compute gradient, step — powers linear regression, neural networks, and the training of giant language models alike. The scale changes; the idea does not.

lessons.title: Evaluating Models: Splits & Metrics
lessons.body:
A model that scores 100% on its training data may be useless — it might have simply MEMORIZED the answers. The only honest test is data it has never seen.

THE TRAIN/TEST SPLIT. Before training, hold back a slice of data (commonly 20%) as a test set. Train on the other 80%, then measure on the held-out 20%. Good score on unseen data = real learning.

```rust
let split = (data.len() as f64 * 0.8) as usize;
let (train, test) = data.split_at(split);
```

OVERFITTING is the villain: the model fits the training noise so closely it fails on anything new. The telltale sign — high training accuracy, low test accuracy. Underfitting is the opposite: too simple to capture the pattern, poor on both.

WHICH METRIC? Depends on the task:

• Classification → ACCURACY (fraction correct). But beware imbalance: if 99% of emails are "not spam", a model that always says "not spam" scores 99% while being worthless. Then reach for precision and recall.
• Regression (predicting numbers) → MEAN SQUARED ERROR (MSE): average of (predicted − actual)². Penalizes big misses heavily.

```rust
let mse: f64 = preds.iter().zip(&actuals)
    .map(|(p, a)| (p - a).powi(2))
    .sum::<f64>() / preds.len() as f64;
```

The professional habit: never judge a model by its training score. Split first, evaluate on the test set, and watch the GAP between train and test performance — that gap is your overfitting alarm.

lessons.title: Logistic Regression
lessons.body:
Linear regression predicts a NUMBER. But often you want a YES/NO: is this email spam? Will this customer churn? For that, logistic regression bends linear regression into a probability machine.

The trick is one function: the SIGMOID. It squashes any number — from minus a million to plus a million — into the range 0 to 1, which we read as a probability.

```rust
fn sigmoid(x: f64) -> f64 {
    1.0 / (1.0 + (-x).exp())
}
```

Its S-shape: large negative inputs → near 0, large positive → near 1, and 0 → exactly 0.5. So the model computes a linear score (w·x + b) just like before, then passes it through sigmoid to get "probability of yes".

```rust
let score = w * feature + b;
let prob = sigmoid(score);     // e.g. 0.87 -> 87% likely "yes"
let label = if prob >= 0.5 { 1 } else { 0 };
```

The 0.5 THRESHOLD turns the probability into a decision. Raise it (say 0.8) to be more cautious about saying "yes"; lower it to catch more positives.

Training still uses gradient descent — only the loss changes to one suited for probabilities (binary cross-entropy / log loss) instead of squared error.

The big picture: linear regression draws a line to predict values; logistic regression draws a boundary to SEPARATE classes. Same machinery (weights, gradient descent), one extra squashing function, and suddenly you have a classifier.

lessons.title: Numerical Computing with ndarray
lessons.body:
Python has NumPy; Rust has ndarray. When you do ML, you stop thinking in single numbers and start thinking in ARRAYS — vectors and matrices processed all at once. That is the heart of fast numerical code.

A plain Vec<f64> works for a list, but real ML needs n-dimensional arrays with shape, broadcasting and matrix math. The ndarray crate provides Array1 (a vector), Array2 (a matrix), and friends.

```rust
use ndarray::{array, Array2};

let a = array![[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]];   // a 2x2 matrix
let v = array![10.0, 20.0];               // a length-2 vector

let scaled = &a * 2.0;     // every element doubled — "vectorized"
let row_sum = a.sum_axis(ndarray::Axis(1)); // sum across columns
```

The mental shift is VECTORIZATION: instead of a hand-written loop adding numbers one by one, you express the operation on the whole array. It is shorter, clearer, and lets the library use highly optimized routines under the hood.

Matrix multiplication — the single most important ML operation, the core of every neural network layer — is a method call:

```rust
let product = a.dot(&b);   // matrix multiply
```

Why bother when Vec works? Three reasons: shape safety (mismatched dimensions are caught), speed (vectorized, cache-friendly, optionally backed by BLAS), and readability (the code looks like the math). For anything beyond toy examples, reach for ndarray rather than nesting Vecs by hand.

lessons.title: Deploying Models & Inference
lessons.body:
Training a model is half the story. The other half — and where Rust truly shines — is INFERENCE: running a trained model in production, fast and reliably.

TRAINING vs INFERENCE:
• Training: heavy, one-time (or periodic), often done in Python on big GPUs. Computes the weights.
• Inference: lightweight, runs constantly, must be fast and lean. Takes inputs, produces predictions.

Rust's strengths — speed, tiny memory footprint, no garbage-collector pauses, a single self-contained binary — make it ideal for serving models. A common, very practical pattern: train in Python, then run inference in Rust.

How does a Python model reach Rust? Usually through a portable format:

• ONNX — an open standard for models. Export from PyTorch/TensorFlow, then load with the `ort` (ONNX Runtime) crate in Rust.
• Native Rust frameworks — Candle and Burn can load weights and run inference directly, no Python at all.

The inference loop is always the same shape:

```rust
let model = load_model("model.onnx")?;   // once, at startup
loop {
    let input = receive_request();        // get features
    let output = model.run(input)?;       // forward pass
    send_response(output);                // return prediction
}
```

Load once, run many times. Wrap that in a web server (axum, actix) and you have a production ML service in a single fast binary — which is exactly why companies increasingly put Rust on the inference path even when the model was trained elsewhere.

lessons.title: Rust on Microcontrollers
lessons.body:
A microcontroller is a complete tiny computer on one chip — a Raspberry Pi Pico costs a few dollars, runs on milliwatts, and lives inside washing machines, drones, keyboards and rockets. No operating system. No safety net. Your code IS the machine.

That used to mean C, and C's classic crashes. Rust changed the game: the same compiler that catches your bugs in the quiz catches them here — where a bug might mean a stuck motor, not a stack trace.

One new idea: there is no OS, so there is no standard library. Embedded Rust programs start with:

```rust
#![no_std]   // no operating system services
#![no_main]  // we define our own entry point
```

No println!, no files, no heap by default — just your code and the silicon. What replaces it? The embedded ecosystem:

• embedded-hal — THE trick to learn. Traits like "a pin you can set high/low". Write a sensor driver against the trait and it runs unchanged on a Pico, an ESP32, or an STM32 — like a phone charger standard for code.
• Embassy — the modern async framework: await a button press while blinking an LED, no threads needed.
• probe-rs — one `cargo run` flashes the chip and streams logs back.

Boards to start with: Raspberry Pi Pico (RP2040/RP2350) or ESP32 — both have first-class Rust support (esp-rs is Espressif's official SDK).

And the eternal first program? Not Hello World — there's no screen! It's blinky: make an LED blink. That's your project.

lessons.title: Sensors, ADC & PWM
lessons.body:
Digital pins only know ON and OFF. The real world is analog — temperatures, light levels, knob positions. Two converters bridge the gap:

ADC (Analog → Digital): "how much?" as a number. A 12-bit ADC reports 0–4095, where 0 = 0V and 4095 = 3.3V. Your job is converting that raw count into real units:

```rust
let raw = 2048u16;            // ADC reading
let volts = raw as f32 / 4095.0 * 3.3;
let temp_c = (volts - 0.5) * 100.0; // sensor's formula
```

That formula comes from the sensor's datasheet — the instruction manual of hardware. Reading datasheets is half of embedded work.

PWM (the reverse trick): chips can't output "half voltage", so they fake it — switching ON/OFF thousands of times a second. The fraction of time spent ON is the duty cycle:

• 100% duty = fully on
• 50% duty = half brightness
• 10% duty = a dim glow

PWM dims LEDs, sets motor speeds, and steers servo arms. Brightness knob = ADC in, PWM out — exactly your project.

(In production you'd read sensors over I2C or SPI buses with an embedded-hal driver crate — same ideas, shared wires.)
