lessons.title: Interrupts & Real-Time
lessons.body:
How does a chip notice a button press? Two philosophies:

Polling — check the pin in a loop, thousands of times a second. It's walking to the front door every five seconds to see if someone's there. Works, but burns cycles and can still MISS a fast press between checks.

Interrupts — install a doorbell. The hardware itself watches the pin; the instant it changes, your normal code is paused, a special function runs, then normal code resumes:

```rust
#[interrupt]
fn GPIO_IRQ() {
    // the doorbell rang — handle it!
    PRESSED.store(true, Ordering::Relaxed);
}
```

That function is an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine), and it comes with one iron rule: keep it SHORT. While the ISR runs, everything else is on hold — set a flag, record a timestamp, get out. The main loop (or an Embassy task) does the real work later.

Notice the sharing problem: the ISR and main loop both touch PRESSED — two contexts, shared data, the borrow checker's eyebrow rises. Embedded answers: atomics (as above) for simple flags, or critical sections (briefly disable interrupts) for bigger data. Mutex thinking, bare-metal edition.

Now the classic gotcha that bites EVERY first hardware project: bounce. A physical button doesn't click once — its metal contacts ricochet, electrically "pressing" 5-10 times within a few milliseconds. Your counter says 7 presses; your finger says 1.

The fix is debouncing: after accepting an edge, ignore further edges for ~20-50ms. One timestamp comparison — and your project implements exactly that filter, on a recorded burst of bouncy edges.

project.description: Real recorded edges from a bouncy button — turn them into true press counts. The 50ms-window logic is yours to write; then experiment: what window is too short (bounces leak through) or too long (fast double-clicks merge)?

questions.explanation: Hardware watches the pin and calls you the instant it changes — no cycles wasted checking, no fast press missed between checks.

questions.explanation: The ISR borrows the whole CPU. Set a flag, stamp a time, leave — let the main loop do real work on its own schedule.

lessons.title: Capstone: Weather Station
lessons.body:
The embedded finale — assembling every lesson into one real device: a desk weather station on a Raspberry Pi Pico.

The hardware bill (under $20): a Pico, a BME280 sensor (temperature + humidity + pressure in one chip), a photoresistor for light, and an LED for alerts.

Now watch each lesson click into place:

• The BME280 speaks I2C — a two-wire bus where digital sensors deliver clean readings. You don't bit-bang it: an embedded-hal driver crate handles the protocol, and because it's written against the hal TRAITS, the same driver runs on Pico, ESP32, or STM32 (lesson 1's promise, kept).
• The photoresistor is analog — your ADC lesson: raw counts → voltage → "bright/dim".
• The alert LED breathes via PWM — duty cycle as brightness.
• The architecture is Embassy tasks, one honest loop each:

```rust
#[embassy_executor::task]   // every 60s
async fn sensor_task(...) { /* read, send */ }

#[embassy_executor::task]   // owns the state
async fn brain_task(...) { /* receive, decide */ }
```

• Tasks talk through a channel (Embassy has them too — your channels lesson, no_std edition). Sensor task SENDS readings; brain task OWNS the state. No shared mutable anything.
• The brain is a state machine — enum Mode { Normal, HeatAlert, Dark } with match-driven transitions. Lesson GPIO's pattern, running a real product.
• Logs stream to your laptop over the debug probe via defmt — embedded's println.

That's a real IoT device: ~150 lines of safe Rust, months on a battery (Embassy sleeping between readings), no OS anywhere. Your project simulates the brain — the decision core you'd flash to the real thing.

lessons.title: no_std & the Core Library
lessons.body:
A microcontroller has no operating system, often just a few kilobytes of RAM, and no heap by default. So the usual Rust standard library — which assumes files, threads, an allocator and an OS — simply cannot run. The answer is no_std.

At the top of an embedded program you write:

```rust
#![no_std]
#![no_main]
```

`#![no_std]` says "do not link the full standard library". Instead you get `core` — the subset that needs no operating system: integers, floats, slices, Option, Result, iterators, Ordering. All the language fundamentals, none of the OS-dependent parts.

What you LOSE without std:
• No String or Vec (they need a heap allocator).
• No println! (there is no console to print to).
• No std::fs, std::net, std::thread.

What you KEEP with core:
• &str and array/slice operations.
• Option and Result and the ? operator.
• All arithmetic, traits, generics, pattern matching.

Need a growable Vec on a chip that DOES have some RAM? Add the `alloc` crate and a global allocator — then Vec and String come back, opt-in. Many embedded projects skip even that, using fixed-size buffers with crates like `heapless` (a Vec with a compile-time capacity, no heap at all).

The mindset shift: embedded Rust is the SAME language with a smaller library and no hidden allocations. Every byte is accounted for, which is exactly what you want when the whole computer fits on a fingernail.

lessons.title: Memory-Mapped I/O & Registers
lessons.body:
How does code turn on an LED or read a button? Through REGISTERS — special memory addresses wired directly to the hardware. On a microcontroller, talking to a pin is literally writing a number to a specific address.

This is MEMORY-MAPPED I/O: peripherals (GPIO, timers, UART) appear as if they were memory. Write a bit to address 0x4002_0014 and a physical pin goes high. Read address 0x4002_0010 and you learn which buttons are pressed. The CPU has no special "talk to hardware" instructions — it just reads and writes these magic addresses.

A register is usually 32 bits, where each bit (or group of bits) controls something:

```
GPIO output register (conceptual):
  bit 0 -> pin 0   bit 1 -> pin 1   ...
  writing 1 = high, 0 = low
```

Setting pin 5 high without disturbing the others means flipping ONE bit — classic bit manipulation:

```rust
// set bit 5
reg |= 1 << 5;
// clear bit 5
reg &= !(1 << 5);
// test bit 3
let pressed = (reg >> 3) & 1 == 1;
```

Doing this by raw address is error-prone and `unsafe`. So in real Rust you almost never touch addresses directly. Instead:

• A PAC (Peripheral Access Crate), auto-generated per chip, gives each register a typed name and safe-ish methods.
• A HAL (Hardware Abstraction Layer) wraps the PAC in friendly APIs like `led.set_high()`.

Underneath, set_high() is still flipping a bit in a memory-mapped register — the HAL just makes it safe, readable, and impossible to point at the wrong address. Understanding the bit-twiddling underneath is what makes those tidy method calls click.

lessons.title: I2C & SPI Buses
lessons.body:
UART connects two devices. But a real board might have a temperature sensor, a display, an accelerometer and a memory chip — all sharing the same few wires. For that you need a BUS: I2C or SPI.

I2C — two wires, many devices. Just SDA (data) and SCL (clock) shared by everyone. Each device has a unique ADDRESS (like a house number). The controller calls out an address; only the matching device responds.

```rust
// read 1 byte from the sensor at address 0x48
let mut buf = [0u8; 1];
i2c.write_read(0x48, &[register], &mut buf)?;
```

• Pros: only two wires no matter how many devices; built-in addressing.
• Cons: slower; the shared bus can get crowded.

SPI — four wires, blazing fast. SCLK (clock), MOSI (controller→device), MISO (device→controller), and a CS (chip-select) line PER device. To talk to a device you pull its CS low, exchange bytes, then release it.

```rust
cs.set_low();                       // select this device
spi.transfer_in_place(&mut buffer)?; // full-duplex byte swap (embedded-hal 1.0)
cs.set_high();                      // done
```

• Pros: very fast, full-duplex (send and receive at once).
• Cons: more wires — every extra device needs its own CS line.

The rule of thumb: I2C when you have many slow-ish devices and want to save pins (sensors, small displays); SPI when you need speed (fast displays, SD cards, flash memory). Rust's embedded-hal traits abstract both, so a driver written against the trait works on any chip — write a sensor driver once, run it everywhere. (Rust's embedded-hal makes this possible.)

lessons.title: Project Structure & Modules
lessons.body:
Open any serious Rust repo on GitHub and you'll see the same skeleton. Learn it once, feel at home everywhere:

```rust
my_app/
├── Cargo.toml        // the manifest (ID card + shopping list)
├── Cargo.lock        // exact versions, auto-managed
├── src/
│   ├── main.rs       // binary entry point
│   ├── lib.rs        // library root (the real logic)
│   ├── db.rs         // module: my_app's database code
│   └── api/          // bigger module as a folder
│       ├── mod.rs
│       └── users.rs
├── tests/            // integration tests
└── examples/         // runnable usage examples
```

The pro pattern: keep main.rs TINY — it just calls into lib.rs. Why? Everything in lib.rs can be tested and reused; main.rs is just the ignition key.

Inside files, code is organized with modules — think departments in a company:

```rust
mod inventory {
    pub fn count() -> u32 { 42 }
    fn secret_audit() {}      // private!
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", inventory::count());
}
```

Two rules carry you far:

• Everything is PRIVATE by default. `pub` is the keyword for "other departments may use this". Small public surface = freedom to refactor the rest.
• Paths use `::` — `crate::api::users::create` reads like a file path for code. `use` creates shortcuts: `use crate::api::users;`

A folder becomes a module via `mod.rs` (or a same-named .rs file next to it). That's the whole system — no magic, just files and two keywords.

lessons.title: Cargo.toml, Dependencies & Releases
lessons.body:
Cargo.toml is your project's ID card and shopping list in one file:

```rust
[package]
name = "rustquest"
version = "1.2.3"
edition = "2021"

[dependencies]
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
tokio = "1"

[profile.release]
opt-level = 3
```

The shopping list uses semver — version numbers with grammar: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (1.2.3):

• PATCH bump (1.2.4) = bug fix, safe
• MINOR bump (1.3.0) = new features, still compatible
• MAJOR bump (2.0.0) = breaking changes — read the changelog!

Writing "1.0" means "any compatible 1.x" — Cargo picks the newest, then Cargo.lock freezes the EXACT versions so your teammate and your server build the same thing. (Commit the lockfile for apps.)

The single most important production fact:

```rust
cargo build            // DEBUG: fast compile, slow code
cargo build --release  // RELEASE: optimized, 10-100x faster
```

Shipping a debug build is the classic rookie mistake — Rust's famous speed lives behind that flag.

The daily pro toolbelt: cargo fmt (formats code — no style arguments), cargo clippy (catches 700+ common mistakes with advice), cargo test, cargo doc. Run fmt + clippy + test before every commit and you're already working like a Rust team.

lessons.title: Production Error Handling
lessons.body:
In the quiz lessons, .unwrap() was fine. In production, unwrap is a landmine: the moment that "can't happen" case happens at 3am, your service dies with a panic. Production rule number one:

Library and server code returns Result — it never decides to crash on the caller's behalf.

```rust
fn read_port(cfg: &str) -> Result<u16, String> {
    cfg.trim()
       .parse()
       .map_err(|_| format!("bad port: {cfg}"))
}
```

The caller decides what failure means: retry? default? log and continue? That's the whole philosophy — errors are VALUES you handle, not explosions you survive.

The ? operator keeps this from getting verbose — it means "if this failed, pass the error up; otherwise unwrap and continue":

```rust
fn load() -> Result<Config, String> {
    let text = read_file("app.toml")?;  // may bail
    let cfg = parse(&text)?;            // may bail
    Ok(cfg)
}
```

Three lines, two failure points, zero boilerplate.

In real codebases two tiny crates complete the picture:
• anyhow — for applications: one flexible error type, add context with .context("loading config")
• thiserror — for libraries: define precise error enums users can match on

lessons.title: CI/CD, Docker & Deployment
lessons.body:
You've built the quality tools — fmt, clippy, test. CI (Continuous Integration) is the robot teammate who runs ALL of them on EVERY push, before code can merge. Nobody forgets, nobody skips, nothing broken lands on main.

On GitHub this is a small YAML file (.github/workflows/ci.yml):

```rust
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: cargo fmt --check
      - run: cargo clippy -- -D warnings
      - run: cargo test
```

Read it as a checklist: formatting clean? No clippy warnings (-D promotes them to errors)? All tests green? Any step fails → the pull request gets a red ❌ and can't merge. Your project's immune system.

CD (Continuous Deployment) is the next robot: when main goes green, build the release and ship it. And here Rust hands you a gift most languages can't: `cargo build --release` produces ONE self-contained binary. No interpreter, no node_modules, no runtime to install — copy the file, run it.

That gift makes Docker images comically small via multi-stage builds: stage 1 is a fat builder image that compiles; stage 2 starts from a tiny base and copies in ONLY the binary. Python images: often 1GB+. Rust images: can be 10-20MB.

Cross-compilation rounds it out: `cargo build --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` builds for a Raspberry Pi from your laptop. One codebase, binaries for every machine — including that Pico from the embedded course.

lessons.title: Logging & Tracing
lessons.body:
In production you cannot attach a debugger to a running server. Your eyes are the LOGS — and good logging is the difference between fixing an incident in minutes versus hours.

The amateur move is println! everywhere. The professional move is a logging facade with LEVELS. Rust uses the `log` crate (or the richer `tracing`) to mark each message with severity:

```rust
use log::{info, warn, error, debug};

info!("server started on port {port}");
warn!("retrying request, attempt {n}");
error!("payment failed: {err}");
debug!("cache hit ratio: {ratio}");
```

The levels, loudest to quietest: ERROR > WARN > INFO > DEBUG > TRACE. The magic is that you choose at RUNTIME how much to show. In production, set the level to INFO and the noisy debug lines vanish — no code changes, just an environment variable:

```
RUST_LOG=info cargo run
RUST_LOG=debug cargo run   // when chasing a bug
```

Why a FACADE? The `log` crate only defines the macros; you plug in a backend (`env_logger`, `tracing-subscriber`) that decides where logs go — terminal, file, or a JSON stream to a log aggregator. Your library code logs without caring where it lands.

For services, `tracing` adds SPANS — structured context that follows a request across function calls, so you can see the whole journey of request #4837 through your system. STRUCTURED logging (key-value fields, often JSON) then lets tools search and graph your logs.

The rule: log at the right level, include the values you will wish you had (ids, counts, errors), and never log secrets like passwords or tokens.

lessons.title: Configuration & Environment
lessons.body:
The same binary should run on your laptop, in staging, and in production — without recompiling. The thing that changes is CONFIGURATION: database URLs, ports, API keys, feature flags. Hard-coding these is a rookie mistake; managing them well is a hallmark of production code.

The guiding principle is the TWELVE-FACTOR rule: store config in the ENVIRONMENT, not in the code. Read it at startup:

```rust
use std::env;

let port = env::var("PORT").unwrap_or_else(|_| "8080".to_string());
let db_url = env::var("DATABASE_URL")
    .expect("DATABASE_URL must be set");
```

Notice the two styles: PORT has a sensible DEFAULT (unwrap_or_else), while DATABASE_URL is REQUIRED (expect — fail loudly at startup if missing). Failing fast on missing required config is much better than crashing mysteriously an hour later.

SECRETS — passwords, API keys — deserve special care:
• Never commit them to git. Use a .env file (git-ignored) for local dev, loaded by the `dotenvy` crate.
• In production, inject them through the environment or a secrets manager.

For richer config, crates like `config` and `figment` layer multiple sources — defaults, then a config file, then environment variables, then command-line flags — each overriding the last. And `serde` can deserialize a whole TOML/YAML/JSON file straight into a typed struct:

```rust
#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct Settings { port: u16, workers: usize }
```

The payoff: one artifact, many environments. Build once, configure per deployment, keep secrets out of the source — and validate required values at startup so problems surface immediately.

lessons.title: Security & Dependency Auditing
lessons.body:
Rust eliminates whole categories of memory bugs — no buffer overflows, no use-after-free in safe code. But it does NOT make your application automatically secure. The remaining risks come from logic, dependencies, and how you handle untrusted input.

YOUR DEPENDENCIES are a major surface. A typical project pulls in dozens of crates; any one could have a known vulnerability. Two essential tools:

```
cargo audit    # checks your deps against the RustSec advisory database
cargo deny     # enforces policy: licenses, banned crates, duplicates
```

Run `cargo audit` in CI so a newly disclosed vulnerability in a dependency fails the build until you update. Keeping `Cargo.lock` committed for applications makes builds reproducible and auditable.

UNTRUSTED INPUT is the other classic danger. Validate everything that comes from outside — users, files, the network:
• Never build SQL by string concatenation; use parameterized queries (sqlx does this and even checks them at compile time).
• Cap sizes (max upload, max string length) to prevent denial-of-service.
• Treat `unwrap()` on external input as a liability — a malformed request should return an error, not panic the server.

THE `unsafe` KEYWORD deserves respect. It does not turn off all checks, but it lets you do things the compiler cannot verify (raw pointers, FFI). Keep unsafe blocks small, documented with a comment explaining WHY they are sound, and audited carefully — most application code needs none.

SECRETS hygiene rounds it out: no hard-coded keys, no secrets in logs, rotate credentials, and use HTTPS/TLS. Rust gives you a safe foundation; secure software is what you build on top of it with validation, least privilege, and up-to-date dependencies.

lessons.body:
The grand finale of the Rust Book — a web server from raw TCP sockets, no framework. It's the concurrency course wearing work clothes. Layer 1 — accept connections: ```rust use std::net::TcpListener; let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:7878")?; for stream in listener.incoming() { handle(stream?); // each one is a browser! } ``` Layer 2 — speak HTTP. It's just text! A browser sends: ```rust GET /farm HTTP/1.1 Host: localhost:7878 ``` Method, path, version — first line tells you everything needed for routing. You reply in kind: ```rust HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n\r\n

hello!

``` Status line, blank line, body. Route with — what else — a match on (method, path), `_ =>` returning 404. The web demystified: strings in, strings out. Layer 3 — the actual lesson: one thread per connection melts under load (10,000 browsers = 10,000 threads). The fix is a thread pool, and look at the ingredients: spawn N workers ONCE (threads lesson), feed them jobs through a channel (channels lesson), share the receiver with Arc (lesson three). Every worker loops: lock, take a job, release, work. ```rust let job = receiver.lock().unwrap().recv(); ``` Three lessons you already own, composed into real infrastructure. The Playground can't open sockets, so your build implements the brain — request parsing and routing — over recorded requests. The socket part is the two lines above.

lessons.title: Capstone: Expression Calculator
lessons.body:
Time to build a real calculator — one that reads "3 + 4 * 2" and computes the answer. This classic project ties together strings, iterators, enums, and Result, and introduces the idea behind every programming language: turning text into a result.

The pipeline has two stages every interpreter shares:

1. TOKENIZE (lexing) — split the raw text into meaningful pieces called tokens: numbers and operators.

```
"3 + 4" -> [Num(3), Plus, Num(4)]
```

2. EVALUATE — walk the tokens and compute. For a first version we can evaluate left to right; a fuller version respects precedence (× before +).

A clean way to model tokens is an ENUM — exactly the "make illegal states unrepresentable" idea:

```rust
enum Token {
    Num(f64),
    Plus,
    Minus,
    Times,
    Divide,
}
```

Splitting input on whitespace and mapping each piece to a Token is a natural iterator job. Then a fold or a simple loop carries a running total.

The interesting design decisions:
• Use Result to handle BAD input ("3 + +") gracefully instead of panicking — return Err with a helpful message.
• Division by zero is a runtime concern: check the divisor and return an Err rather than producing infinity or panicking.
• Precedence (× and ÷ before + and −) is the natural next step — a two-pass approach (do all the × and ÷ first, then the + and −) is a beginner-friendly way to get it right.

This is your first taste of building a tiny LANGUAGE. The same tokenize-then-evaluate shape scales all the way up to real compilers and the calculator app on your phone. Start with whitespace-separated tokens and left-to-right evaluation; once that works, add precedence and error handling. Build it in small, testable steps — that habit matters more than any single feature.

lessons.title: Capstone: Word Frequency Analyzer
lessons.body:
Build a tool that reads text and reports the most common words — the engine behind word clouds, search ranking, and basic text analytics. It is a perfect showcase for HashMap, iterators, and sorting working together.

The plan, in four moves:

1. NORMALIZE — lowercase the text and strip punctuation so "Rust," and "rust" count as the same word.

```rust
let cleaned: String = text.chars()
    .map(|c| if c.is_alphanumeric() || c.is_whitespace() { c } else { ' ' })
    .collect::<String>()
    .to_lowercase();
```

2. COUNT — tally each word with the HashMap entry API (the canonical counting pattern):

```rust
let mut counts: HashMap<&str, u32> = HashMap::new();
for word in cleaned.split_whitespace() {
    *counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1;
}
```

3. SORT — a HashMap is unordered, so to find the top words, collect the entries into a Vec and sort by count descending:

```rust
let mut pairs: Vec<(&str, u32)> = counts.into_iter().collect();
pairs.sort_by(|a, b| b.1.cmp(&a.1));   // highest count first
```

4. REPORT — take the top N and print them.

The skills on display: the entry API for counting, the "collect a map into a Vec to sort it" idiom (since maps cannot be sorted in place), and sort_by with a custom comparator. A nice extension is filtering out STOP WORDS (the, a, is) that dominate every text but carry little meaning — just skip them while counting.

This pattern — normalize, count, rank — is the foundation of real text processing. Search engines rank documents by word importance; spam filters weigh word frequencies; your phone's autocomplete learns from them. You are building the core loop of all of it. Tackle it one stage at a time, printing intermediate results to confirm each step before moving on.

project.title: Add a versioned event
project.description: Add a `NetworkChanged` variant to a small event enum, give it an optional field with skip_serializing_if, and assert the JSON shape in a test. This is the same change you make when a new adapter starts emitting something.

lessons.body:
Most of bread is a message pipeline: adapters turn kernel or compositor facts into one shared type, and everything else consumes it.

`bread-shared` defines those wire types once so `breadd`, the module host and the CLI cannot drift apart:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct Device {
    pub id: String,
    pub name: String,
    pub device: String,
    pub subsystem: String,
    #[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]
    pub vendor_id: Option<String>,
    #[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]
    pub product_id: Option<String>,
}
```

Two habits make this durable:

- **Optional data is `Option<T>` with `skip_serializing_if`.** An event without a vendor id stays small, and a reader built earlier simply sees a missing key.
- **Enums carry the kind.** The module-host push envelope is an internally tagged enum, so the tag travels next to the payload:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(tag = "push")]
pub enum ModuleHostPush {
    #[serde(rename = "event")]
    Event { subscription_id: String, event: BreadEvent },
    #[serde(rename = "timer")]
    Timer { timer_id: String },
}
```

That serialises as `{"push":"event", ...}` or `{"push":"timer", ...}`. In Rust, `match` on it is exhaustive: adding a variant forces every consumer to handle it instead of silently dropping a message.

Deserialisation is forgiving by default: unknown keys are ignored, and a missing optional key becomes `None`. Add `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` only when you want the opposite, which is usually for hand-written config, not for events on the wire.

options: To omit the key when there is no value
To rename the field on the wire

questions.explanation: The tag value is the renamed variant name, and the fields sit beside it.

lessons.title: One state, many readers
lessons.body:
`breadd` keeps one `RuntimeState` behind a lock and hands clones of a handle to adapters:

```rust
#[derive(Clone)]
pub struct StateHandle {
    state: Arc<RwLock<RuntimeState>>,
    command_tx: mpsc::UnboundedSender<StateCommand>,
}
```

`Arc` shares ownership; `RwLock` allows many readers or one writer. The daemon uses `tokio::sync::RwLock` because guards are taken inside async code.

The rules that keep this healthy:

- **Never hold a `std::sync::MutexGuard` across `.await`.** The guard is not `Send`, so the compiler usually stops you, but the temptation to leak it into a helper is real.
- **Keep the critical section short.** Build the value you need, drop the guard, then do I/O or send it on a channel.
- **Do not take a read guard and then a write guard in the same task.** Tokio's writer-preferring lock will deadlock while you wait for readers to drain, and you are the reader.

Reading a path snapshots the state once and walks plain JSON afterwards:

```rust
pub async fn state_get(&self, path: &str) -> Option<Value> {
    let state = self.state.read().await;
    let full = serde_json::to_value(&*state).ok()?;
    // walk `full` by dots, then clone the leaf
    Some(current.clone())
}
```

Mutations do not scatter write locks through the code base. They are messages to one owner:

```rust
pub enum StateCommand {
    RegisterSubscription { id: SubscriptionId, pattern: String, once: bool },
    RemoveSubscription { id: SubscriptionId },
    SetProfile { name: String },
}
```

A single consumer applies commands in order, which removes lock-ordering puzzles and makes the state transitions easy to test.

project.title: Wrap the error chain
project.description: Take the small function below, replace the bare `?` with context that names the file being read, and make the CLI print the whole chain with `{:#}`. Run it against a missing path.

lessons.body:
A daemon runs unattended, so an error message is a user interface: it has to say what failed, where, and whether retrying is sensible.

Two crates cover almost everything:

- `thiserror` for library errors with a real type and variants callers can match.
- `anyhow` at application edges, where the only job is to carry context to a log or a CLI.

```rust
fn read_config(path: &Path) -> Result<Config> {
    let text = fs::read_to_string(path)
        .with_context(|| format!("reading {}", path.display()))?;
    toml::from_str(&text)
        .with_context(|| format!("parsing {}", path.display()))
}
```

`?` converts the error with `From`, which is why `io::Error` and `toml::Error` both flow into `anyhow::Error`. The chain keeps both layers; `{:#}` prints it on one line, and `%err` in a tracing field prints the top message while the chain remains available.

Classify before you retry:

- **Recoverable:** a socket closed, a device disappeared, a temporary permission failure. Log with structure, back off, retry.
- **Fatal:** a config file that does not parse, a missing binary, an unsupported kernel feature. Exit with a message the user can act on.

```rust
error!(adapter = name, error = %err, "adapter task failed");
```

Avoid string matching on error text. If a caller must branch, give it a typed error via `thiserror`. And keep `.unwrap()` out of request paths: a panic in a daemon is an outage, not a test failure.

When error types must be strings

lessons.title: Unix sockets and JSON envelopes
lessons.body:
`breadd` exposes a Unix socket for the CLI, the bar and the module host. The protocol is deliberately boring: one JSON document per line.

Requests and responses share an id:

```json
{"id":7,"method":"state.get","params":{"path":"power"}}
{"id":7,"result":{"online":true}}
{"id":7,"error":"unknown path"}
```

Unsolicited pushes are tagged so they can never be mistaken for a response:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(tag = "push")]
pub enum ModuleHostPush {
    #[serde(rename = "event")]
    Event { subscription_id: String, event: BreadEvent },
    #[serde(rename = "timer")]
    Timer { timer_id: String },
}
```

A response envelope never carries a `push` key, so one `match` on the tag is enough to demultiplex a connection that is doing both request/response and event delivery.

Practical rules:

- **Frame on newlines.** `serde_json` escapes newlines inside strings, so a JSON document never contains a raw line break. `read_line` plus `serde_json::from_str` is a complete framer.
- **Always time out.** A peer that stops reading must not stall the daemon. Wrap reads in `tokio::time::timeout`, then close the connection.
- **Handshake version.** The module host sends a one-time token and receives `{module, permissions, api_version}`. Reject a mismatch before accepting work.
- **Do not trust the client's identity.** The daemon decides which module a token belongs to; the child does not get to assert it.

The real implementation also separates ownership with `UnixStream::into_split`, so the reader and writer can live in different tasks without a mutex.

lessons.title: Hosting Lua modules safely
lessons.body:
Modules are Lua, the daemon is Rust. `mlua` (0.9, `lua54`, `vendored`, `async`, `serialize`) is the bridge.

Inside the process, a module registers handlers that call back into Rust:

```rust
let handler: Function = /* a Lua function */;
let key = lua.create_registry_value(handler)?;   // keep it alive
let func: Function = lua.registry_value(&key)?;  // fetch it later
```

`RegistryKey` is how a callback survives after the Lua stack frame that produced it. Conversions use `LuaSerdeExt` so a serde struct becomes a table and back without hand-written marshalling.

Errors must cross the boundary in the right type:

```rust
let value = engine
    .lookup(path)
    .map_err(LuaError::external)?;   // Rust error -> Lua error
```

`LuaError::external` boxes the Rust error so the script sees a normal Lua failure with the original message, while the daemon still logs the typed error.

The harder boundary is trust:

- A module declares filesystem and command permissions in its manifest; the host enforces them.
- Out-of-process modules run in `bread-module-host`, confined with Landlock, so a bug or a hostile script cannot read arbitrary files or crash the daemon.
- Validate ids, paths and sizes at the Rust edge. A Lua table can contain anything.
- `mlua::Lua` is not `Sync`; keep it on one task and talk to it through channels instead of sharing it in an `Arc`.

The payoff is a fast extension language with a Rust core that stays in control of capabilities.

[Install]

lessons.body:
The last mile is operational: tests, logs, a unit file and a package that can be trusted.

**Tests.** Keep the logic pure enough to test without sleeping. The glob matcher and the freeze watchdog both take time or names as inputs, so the tests do not need a running compositor. `cargo test` plus `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` is the gate before packaging.

**Logs.** `tracing` with structured fields beats string concatenation:

```rust
info!(adapter = "hyprland", socket = %path.display(), "connected");
error!(adapter = name, error = %err, "adapter task failed");
```

`RUST_LOG=info,breadd=debug` filters at runtime. The journal captures stdout and stderr, so a user can read the same lines with `journalctl --user -u breadd`.

**A user unit:**

```ini
[Unit]
Description=bread daemon
After=graphical-session.target

[Service]
ExecStart=%h/.local/bin/breadd
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2
Environment=RUST_LOG=info

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target
```

`%h` expands to the user's home directory. `Restart=on-failure` restarts after a crash or non-zero exit, not after a clean shutdown. `WantedBy=default.target` makes `systemctl --user enable breadd` start it at login.

**Shutdown.** systemd sends SIGTERM. Translate it into the same shutdown flag the supervisor watches, give adapters a moment to stop, and exit zero. A daemon that ignores SIGTERM gets killed after `TimeoutStopSec`, which loses state.

**Packaging.** bakery pins a version plus a digest, installs the binary and unit, and never trusts a mutable tag. Release builds keep line tables so crash frames can be symbolised, then the published binary is stripped.

lessons.title: Workspaces and shared crates
lessons.body:
Almost every repo in the ecosystem is a Cargo workspace, not a single crate. `bread` has nine members; `bread-ecosystem` carries a dozen product crates plus shared libraries.

```toml
[workspace]
members = ["bread-shared", "bread-scrub", "breadd", "bread-cli", "xtask"]
resolver = "2"

[workspace.dependencies]
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
tokio = { version = "1.40", features = ["full"] }
anyhow = "1.0"
tracing = "0.1"
```

Members opt in with `serde.workspace = true`. One upgrade moves every crate together, which is how the ecosystem avoids three versions of `serde` in one binary.

Shared behavior lives in path crates:

- `bread-shared`: wire types, glob matching, module permissions.
- `bread-utils`: small helpers used by several apps.
- `bread-theme`: the GTK4 stylesheet and palette every app loads.

`xtask` is a binary crate for repo automation (`cargo xtask ...`), so generator and packaging logic stays Rust instead of drifting shell scripts.

The release profile is deliberate:

```toml
[profile.release]
debug = "line-tables-only"
```

Line tables let breadbug resolve crash frames to files and lines. CI publishes the symbols, then strips the shipped binary so users do not download them. Products that care about size also set `lto` and `strip`.

Rules of thumb: a binary crate stays thin (parse, call the library, map errors), shared types never get copy-pasted between repos, and workspace versions are not allowed to drift per member.

lessons.title: CLIs scripts can trust
lessons.body:
Around nine repos ship a CLI (`bakery`, `bread`, `bread-cli`, `breadbug`, `breadlock`, ...). They share the same contract with scripts and humans.

`clap` 4 with derive is the standard:

```rust
#[derive(clap::Parser)]
#[command(name = "bakery", version)]
struct Cli {
    #[command(subcommand)]
    command: Command,
}

#[derive(clap::Subcommand)]
enum Command {
    Install { package: String },
    Update { #[arg(long)] all: bool, package: Option<String> },
}
```

The behaviours that matter:

- **stdout is data, stderr is diagnostics.** `bakery list --json` emits only JSON on stdout; progress, warnings and prompts go to stderr. A pipe must never receive decorations.
- **Exit codes are part of the interface.** 0 means success; clap reports usage errors as 2; a failed operation exits non-zero with an actionable message.
- **`--json` for machines, readable output by default.**
- **`--dry-run` for anything destructive**, and a printed plan of what would change.
- **Precedence is flags, then environment, then config.** bakery honours `BAKERY_PREFIX`, `BAKERY_BIN_DIR`, `--global`, and `/etc/bakery/config.toml` in that order.

Two habits avoid half-done installs: stage downloads in a temp directory, then rename into place; and never delete user data on `remove` (`bakery remove` leaves data files alone).

For HTTP, `ureq` is enough for one blocking request; `reqwest` is the choice when you need async, rustls, or control over redirects. Either way, set a timeout and treat 4xx differently from 5xx.

questions.explanation: Arguments are parsed first, then the operation runs and its result becomes the exit code.

lessons.title: Services and their contracts
lessons.body:
The ecosystem's services (`breadboard`, `bread-tracker`, `breadbug-server`, `breadcloud`) are axum 0.8 on tokio, with reqwest 0.12 and rustls on the client side.

```rust
async fn get_issue(
    State(app): State<AppState>,
    Path(id): Path<i64>,
) -> Result<Json<Issue>, StatusCode> {
    app.store
        .issue(id)
        .await
        .map(Json)
        .map_err(|_| StatusCode::NOT_FOUND)
}
```

The rules that keep a service trustworthy:

- **4xx is the caller's fault, 5xx is yours.** A validation failure is 400 or 422; a database outage is 500. Never turn a bad request into a 500.
- **Timeouts everywhere.** Client requests, database queries, and background jobs. A hung dependency must not hang the handler.
- **Retry only what is safe.** Idempotent GETs and PUTs can be retried with backoff and a cap; a POST that creates something needs an idempotency key first.
- **Liveness and readiness are different questions.** Liveness: the process is up. Readiness: the database is reachable and migrations ran. BOMS treats missing or stale data as unknown, never healthy.
- **The contract is shared.** `api-schema.toml` and the generated client/UI types keep the Rust API and the TypeScript UI from drifting. Renaming a field is a versioned change, not a refactor.
- **Never log secrets or whole payloads.** breadbug's upload endpoint is https-only, refuses redirects, and verifies an `X-Breadbug-Sha256` header before storing the report.

A service that calls optional enrichment should fail open on that enrichment and closed on authentication.

questions.explanation: The previewed bytes are the sent bytes; both sides verify the hash.

questions.explanation: Parse first, persist second, and only return what was actually stored.

lessons.title: SQLite that survives upgrades
lessons.body:
Six repos store local state in SQLite. The service-side ones (`breadboard`, `bread-tracker`, `breadbug-server`) use sqlx 0.8 with the `sqlite`, `runtime-tokio`, `chrono` and `migrate` features.

```rust
sqlx::query!("INSERT INTO issues (title, state) VALUES (?, ?)", title, state)
    .execute(&pool)
    .await?;
```

The practices that keep a database healthy:

- **WAL and a busy timeout.** SQLite allows one writer. Set `journal_mode = WAL` and a busy timeout so concurrent readers do not fail spuriously.
- **Transactions for multi-step changes.** A half-applied update is worse than a failed one.
- **Migrations are append-only.** `sqlx::migrate!("./migrations")` records what ran. Once an applied migration has shipped, never edit it; add a new file.
- **Index what you filter and sort on.** `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` shows a table scan before production does.
- **UTC in the database, local time at the edge.** Store `chrono::Utc`; format for humans in the UI.
- **Health means the same pool.** A readiness check runs `SELECT 1` through the pool the handlers use, not a separate connection.

For the app-side tools (`breadarr`, `breadmemory`) `rusqlite` with the bundled SQLite is the lighter choice; the same rules apply.

Data files are user data. Removing a package does not delete the database; a migration failure must leave the old file intact.

questions.explanation: The macro embeds the migration files and tracks applied versions.

questions.explanation: Configure the file, connect, apply migrations, then start serving.

lessons.title: Crash reports, symbols and scrubbing
lessons.body:
breadbug is the ecosystem's crash path, and it is built around consent.

A user picks an app, a crash, freeze or behaviour report, and sees a preview: counts per section, what the scrubber replaced, a SHA-256, and the full text on request. The bytes that were previewed are the bytes that are saved or sent. The client re-verifies the hash before upload and the server verifies `X-Breadbug-Sha256` too.

Where the data comes from:

- A bounded per-app store: `~/.local/state/bread/bugstore/apps/<app>/{log,events,markers}.jsonl` with 0700 directories and 0600 files, one previous generation, a global cap and a cap on apps.
- `bug.log`, `bug.logs` and `bug.marker` over IPC, so an app does not need breadd to be alive to report.
- breadd's bus events with allowlisted fields plus its own tracing output.

Freeze detection uses `bug.heartbeat` from the app's main loop. It compares monotonic time against the app's own interval, applies a grace window after suspend or a hotplug, and never signals or kills the process.

Symbolication is a build decision: release profiles keep `debug = "line-tables-only"`, CI publishes symbols and strips the binary, and a panic hook records a backtrace plus a build id so frames can be grouped.

Privacy: `bread-scrub` replaces home paths, tokens and other secrets before the preview. Upload is off by default; with it off nothing touches the network, not even the queue or `history --refresh`. An identical resend returns the original receipt, and a deletion token removes it from the server.

options: The server sees more than the preview

questions.explanation: The report is built and hashed once; the preview and the wire bytes are identical.

questions.explanation: It only records and reports; nothing is signalled.

options: Resolving crash frames to file and line
questions.explanation: Symbols are published separately, so users get readable frames without downloading debug info.

questions.prompt: Build, preview, hash, send.
questions.explanation: Scrubbing and serialization happen before hashing; the hash travels with the bytes.

lessons.title: Channels, tracks and pinned releases
lessons.body:
Bread has two distribution channels and three build tracks, and they answer different questions.

**Channels** are how a binary reaches a user:

- **bakery**: `bakery install <name>`, binaries under `~/.local/bin` (or the configured prefix). A repo is on this channel only when all three exist: a `bakery.toml`, an entry in `bread-ecosystem/registry/bread-ecosystem.toml`, and a release workflow that uploads to `dl.breadway.dev` and regenerates `index.json`.
- **pacman**: a `PKGBUILD` plus a package workflow publishing to the self-hosted `[breadway]` repo. Some products (breadlock) are pacman-only because they install root-owned PAM or system files.

BOS is deliberately a third case: it ships as an ISO via its own release workflow and never carries a `bakery.toml` or `PKGBUILD`.

**Tracks** are which build of a bakery package a user gets:

| Track | Index | Trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| stable | `dl.breadway.dev/index.json` | tag `vX.Y.Z` |
| beta | `dl.breadway.dev/beta/index.json` | tag `vX.Y.Z-rc.N` |
| dev | `dl.breadway.dev/dev/index.json` | push to `main` |

There are no per-track branches; one `main` and the tag decide the track.

Operational rules:

- Pin a version plus a digest and verify the digest before install. Never trust a mutable tag.
- Artifacts are immutable; re-uploading over a published version is a bug.
- `bakery install` runs `doctor` first and refuses when a required system dependency is missing.
- `bakery remove` never deletes data files; user state survives uninstall.
- A release without a tested rollback is not finished.

questions.explanation: The tag triggers the build, upload, and index regeneration that bakery reads.

lessons.title: BOS, Lua and the Hyprland layer
lessons.body:
BOS is Arch plus stock Hyprland configured by `hyprland.lua`, with breadd as a systemd user service and the rest of the ecosystem installed by bakery.

Hyprland's Lua config changes how you call it. Legacy dispatch is parsed as Lua and fails:

```bash
hyprctl dispatch workspace 5          # Lua syntax error
hyprctl dispatch "hl.dsp.focus({ workspace = '5' })"
hyprctl eval "hl.config({ cursor = { zoom_factor = 2 } })"
```

Check stdout for `ok`. The legacy form can exit 0 while doing nothing, so exit status alone is not proof.

Bread modules are Lua with the same event names the daemon dispatches:

```lua
local M = bread.module({ name = "dock", version = "1.0.0" })

function M.on_load()
    bread.on("bread.device.connected", function(event)
        if event.data.device == "usb-dock" then
            bread.exec("~/.config/bread/scripts/dock.sh")
        end
    end)
end

return M
```

Modules live in `~/.config/bread/modules`, hot reload with `bread reload`, and can read state (`bread.state`) or wait for events (`bread.wait`, inside `bread.spawn`).

The session is systemd, not a script pile: a user unit with `WantedBy=default.target`, `Restart=on-failure`, `ExecStart=%h/...`, and `journalctl --user -u breadd` for logs. BOS keeps the stock `hyprland.lua` pristine and appends personal config through `local.lua` with a single `pcall` hook, so updates do not conflict.

lessons.title: Layout, allocators and zero-copy
lessons.body:
Rust's default layout is unspecified. Once memory crosses an FFI boundary or is reinterpreted as bytes, layout becomes part of the contract.

- `#[repr(C)]` gives C field order and padding; use it for FFI structs.
- `#[repr(transparent)]` says a wrapper has exactly the same layout as its field, which is how newtypes stay free.
- `#[repr(packed)]` removes padding. Taking a reference to a packed field is undefined behaviour in general; copy the value out instead.
- `size_of::<T>()`, `align_of::<T>()` and `offset_of!` are the tools for checking assumptions. Alignment is a hard requirement: a `u64` pointer must be 8-byte aligned.

Allocation is explicit:

```rust
use std::alloc::{alloc, dealloc, Layout};

let layout = Layout::new::<[u8; 1024]>();
let ptr = unsafe { alloc(layout) };
// ... use the block ...
unsafe { dealloc(ptr, layout) };
```

`dealloc` must receive the same layout used for `alloc`. A custom `GlobalAlloc` is how an arena or a tracking allocator plugs in; `bumpalo` and `typed-arena` are the usual crates when the whole graph lives for one request or one program phase.

Zero-copy means borrowing the bytes instead of copying them:

- `bytes::Bytes` is a cheap, shared, sliceable byte buffer.
- `bytemuck` safely casts plain-old-data between types and byte slices, checking size and alignment.
- `zerocopy` does the same at compile time for many cases.
- Endianness is not layout: `u32::from_le_bytes` before interpreting network data.

Reinterpreting a `Vec<u8>` as `Vec<u32>` is not a cast; it is a different length, alignment and ownership story. Use a typed parser, `bytemuck::cast_slice`, or copy.

questions.explanation: Packed fields may be unaligned; references assume alignment. Copy the value instead.

questions.explanation: The `u32` needs 4-byte alignment, so the tuple is padded to 8 bytes; layout is not the sum of fields.

lessons.title: macro_rules! in depth
lessons.body:
`macro_rules!` matches tokens, not values. Each rule is `(matcher) => { expansion }`, and the first matching rule wins.

Fragment specifiers decide how much the matcher consumes:

- `$x:expr` a single expression
- `$t:ty` a type
- `$i:ident` an identifier
- `$p:pat` a pattern
- `$b:block` a block
- `$l:literal` a literal
- `$tt:tt` one token tree (the escape hatch)
- `$v:vis`, `$m:meta`, `$it:item`, `$lt:lifetime`, `$s:stmt`

Repetition handles variadic input:

```rust
macro_rules! hashmap {
    ($($k:expr => $v:expr),* $(,)?) => {{
        let mut map = std::collections::HashMap::new();
        $( map.insert($k, $v); )*
        map
    }};
}
```

`$(...),*` means zero or more separated by commas; `$(,)?` allows a trailing comma. The same repetition pattern must appear in the expansion.

Hygiene is the sharp edge. Identifiers created inside the macro do not capture caller variables, and a caller's `map` does not collide with the macro's `map`. But types and paths resolve at the call site, which is why macros refer to their own crate as `$crate::...` instead of assuming a path.

Rules of thumb:

- A function or generic is better unless you need variadic arguments, a DSL, or code generation.
- Keep the matcher narrow (`expr`, `ident`) and use `tt` only when you must.
- Test the error cases; a bad macro error points at the call site, so the matcher should fail early and clearly.
- `#[macro_export]` puts it at the crate root; internal macros use `pub(crate) use`.
- A recursive macro needs a base-case rule and a smaller input each step.

lessons.title: Executors, cancellation and backpressure
lessons.body:
A runtime has two halves: an executor that polls futures, and a reactor that turns I/O and timers into wakeups. Tokio's `#[tokio::main]` builds both.

Key facts that change how you write services:

- `tokio::spawn` requires `Send + 'static`. The future cannot borrow local state across a spawn.
- `spawn_blocking` is for CPU-bound or blocking calls (file I/O, FFI, compression). Blocking a runtime worker starves every task on it.
- `tokio::select!` polls branches and drops the loser. Dropping a future is cancellation. It is only safe if the future is cancel-safe: no half-consumed input, no partially written message.
- `JoinSet` gives structured concurrency: spawn many tasks, await them together, and abort the rest on shutdown.
- Bounded channels provide backpressure. An unbounded channel turns a slow consumer into unbounded memory growth.
- `watch` carries the latest shutdown flag; `CancellationToken` (tokio-util) adds child tokens and cooperative stop.

A cancellation-safe read is one that either completes or leaves the buffer untouched. `read_exact` is not cancel-safe (it may have consumed part of the input); `read` is. Check the docs per operation instead of assuming.

Graceful shutdown pattern:

1. Signal handler (or systemd SIGTERM) flips a `watch` to true.
2. Stop accepting new work.
3. Let in-flight handlers finish, with a deadline.
4. Flush buffers, close sockets, exit zero.

A service that is cancelled mid-write and restarts with a corrupted file has a cancellation bug, not an infrastructure problem.

lessons.title: Async in traits without lying about Send
lessons.body:
Since Rust 1.75 you can write:

```rust
trait Store {
    async fn get(&self, id: u64) -> Option<Item>;
}
```

This desugars to a return-position impl trait (RPITIT), not to a boxed future. Two consequences follow.

**Not dyn-compatible.** `dyn Store` cannot exist because each implementor returns a different anonymous future type. Options:

- Keep generics (`fn serve<S: Store>(store: S)`), which monomorphises and is fastest.
- Use `async-trait`, which boxes the future (`Pin<Box<dyn Future>>`) and makes the trait dyn-compatible at the cost of an allocation and a vtable.
- Box by hand: `fn get(&self, id: u64) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = Option<Item>> + Send + '_>>`.

**`Send` is not implied.** An `async fn` in a trait can capture non-`Send` state, so a spawned task cannot assume the returned future is `Send`. The clean fix is the `trait-variant` crate, which generates a second `Send` variant of the trait. Or write the return type explicitly:

```rust
fn get(&self, id: u64) -> impl Future<Output = Option<Item>> + Send;
```

Choosing between designs:

- Generics when you control the call site and want zero cost.
- `Box<dyn Trait>` when you need a runtime registry of implementations (plugins, adapters).
- Boxed futures when the trait must be dyn-compatible.
- An enum of concrete types when the set is closed; it avoids both boxes and dyn.

The mistake to avoid is writing an async trait, spawning its futures, and discovering the `Send` bound only when the service is wired together.

lessons.title: File descriptors, syscalls and sandboxes
lessons.body:
Below `std` sits the kernel interface. Knowing it explains most daemon bugs.

- **File descriptors are owned resources.** `OwnedFd` closes on drop; `BorrowedFd` does not. `AsFd`/`AsRawFd` are the conversion traits. Duplicating with `try_clone` is explicit; `O_CLOEXEC` prevents leaks into children.
- **Syscalls return errors, not exceptions.** `EINTR` means retry. Short reads and writes are normal; loop until the buffer is done. `std::io::Read::read_exact` exists for a reason.
- **Readiness is not completion.** `epoll` says a descriptor is ready; the actual read can still block or return `EAGAIN`. Edge-triggered mode requires draining until `EAGAIN`.
- **Signals are global state.** A handler may only do async-signal-safe work. The usual design is `signalfd` (or a self-pipe) plus a normal event loop, not logic inside the handler.
- **Sandboxing is layered.** `seccomp` filters syscalls, Landlock restricts filesystem access from inside the process, namespaces isolate mounts/pids/network, and capabilities drop root powers. A module host wants all four, in that order.

Crates: `rustix` for a safe syscall wrapper, `nix` for POSIX ergonomics, `libc` when you need the raw call, `signal-hook` for signals, `tokio` for async readiness.

```rust
use std::os::fd::{AsFd, OwnedFd};

fn read_all(fd: &OwnedFd, buf: &mut [u8]) -> std::io::Result<usize> {
    // loop on EINTR and short reads in real code
    rustix::io::read(fd.as_fd(), buf).map_err(Into::into)
}
```

The bread module host is this lesson in production: a child process, a capability manifest, Landlock rules, and an IPC protocol that assumes the child is hostile.

lessons.title: Performance is a measurement discipline
lessons.body:
Optimising without a profile is guessing. The workflow is always: measure, change one thing, measure again.

- Build release. Debug builds skip inlining and bounds-check elision and can be 10 to 100 times slower.
- Use `criterion` for microbenchmarks; it warms up, runs many iterations, and reports confidence intervals.
- `cargo flamegraph` or `perf record` shows where time actually goes. `perf stat` shows cache misses, branch misses and instructions per cycle.
- `heaptrack` and `dhat` find allocation hot spots. Allocation is often the real cost, not arithmetic.

Common wins, in order of frequency:

- **Allocation:** `Vec::with_capacity`, reuse buffers, `Cow<str>` instead of `String`, `SmallVec` for small collections, arenas for request-scoped graphs.
- **I/O:** buffer reads, batch small writes, avoid per-item fsync, use `BufWriter`.
- **Data layout:** struct-of-arrays for hot loops, fewer pointer indirections, smaller enums.
- **Bounds checks:** usually negligible; when they matter, iterate with iterators (which elide them) before reaching for `get_unchecked`.
- **Compile flags:** LTO for cross-crate inlining, codegen-units=1 for a final build, PGO for a known workload.
- **SIMD:** `memchr`, `bytecount`, or explicit `std::simd` (nightly) when a profiler says the loop is hot.

`std::hint::black_box` prevents the optimiser from deleting benchmark work.

Do not trade safety for speed without a measurement and a comment. An `unsafe` fast path that is not faster is pure risk.

lessons.title: Testing beyond example tests
lessons.body:
Example tests prove the cases you thought of. Mature Rust projects add layers for the cases you did not.

- **Unit tests** next to the code, testing pure decisions. Make time, randomness and I/O injectable so tests need no sleeps.
- **Integration tests** in `tests/`, exercising the public API or a running binary.
- **Doc tests** in examples and API docs; they compile, so examples cannot rot.
- **Property tests** (`proptest`, `quickcheck`) generate inputs and shrink failures to a minimal case. Ideal for parsers, codecs, state machines.
- **Fuzzing** (`cargo-fuzz`, libFuzzer) explores byte inputs; a corpus plus a time budget finds panics and hangs.
- **Concurrency tests** (`loom`) model interleavings for lock-free or channel code; they are slow, so test the primitives, not everything.
- **Compile-fail tests** (`trybuild`) pin macro diagnostics.
- **Snapshot tests** (`insta`) are good for rendered output, JSON and CLI help.
- **Mocks** (`mockall`) at trait boundaries, sparingly; fakes with real behaviour age better.

For a daemon, the highest-value tests are usually pure functions extracted from the runtime: the glob matcher, the freeze decision, the state transition, the protocol parser. If a test needs `sleep(100ms)`, the design probably hides a dependency.

Determinism is a feature: `tokio::time::pause` advances a virtual clock, an injected `Clock` trait replaces `Instant::now`, and a seeded RNG makes a flaky test reproducible.

Coverage (`cargo llvm-cov`) tells you what ran, not what is correct. Treat a coverage number as a hint, never a target.

questions.explanation: Fuzzing explores byte inputs and finds panics and hangs that examples miss.

questions.explanation: It is slow and flaky; inject the clock or use deterministic runtime time.

questions.explanation: It compiles fixture files and compares the compiler output.

questions.prompt: Test from cheap to expensive.
questions.explanation: Fast, deterministic tests first; expensive exploration last.

lessons.title: Debugging a running service
lessons.body:
When a daemon misbehaves in production, the evidence is a stack trace, a log, a metric or a core dump, not a debugger attached to your laptop.

**Crashes.** Set `RUST_BACKTRACE=full` for a local reproduction. In production, a panic hook writes the backtrace and build id to the bug store, and breadbug ships it. A core dump (`coredumpctl`, `gdb ./binary core`) gives registers and frames; `addr2line` or `rust-gdb` resolves addresses when symbols are published. Keep line tables in release builds and strip only after publishing symbols.

**Hangs and races.** `tokio-console` shows live tasks, their states and where they are parked. `strace -f -p` shows syscalls; `perf top` shows CPU. A deadlock usually has an obvious lock-ordering cycle once you see the two stacks. For code that must be provably race-free, model it in `loom`.

**Logs and spans.** `tracing` spans carry request or connection ids; `RUST_LOG` filters without recompiling. Log decisions with structured fields:

```rust
warn!(adapter = name, attempt, delay_ms, "restarting after failure");
```

**Metrics.** Counters and histograms answer "how often" and "how slow"; logs answer "what happened to this one". Alert on symptoms (error rate, latency, queue depth), not on every internal event. Distinguish liveness from readiness, and treat missing data as unknown.

**Incident loop.** Stabilise, gather, reproduce, fix, add a regression test, write down the cause. The last two are what stop the same incident from returning.

lessons.title: APIs that are hard to misuse
lessons.body:
A good Rust API makes invalid states unrepresentable and breaking changes explicit.

- **Newtypes** add meaning and invariants: `struct UserId(u64)` cannot be confused with `OrderId`.
- **Private fields plus constructors** let you enforce invariants. A `NonEmpty<T>` that can only be built from a checked slice is worth more than a comment.
- **Enums over booleans** when a third state is plausible; `Option<Option<T>>` is a warning sign.
- **`#[non_exhaustive]`** on public enums and structs reserves the right to add variants and fields without a major version.
- **Sealed traits** (`pub trait Foo: private::Sealed`) let you add methods without downstream implementors breaking.
- **Errors are API.** A typed error with variants is matchable; a `String` is not. `thiserror` for libraries, `anyhow` at the binary edge.
- **Semver:** adding an enum variant without `#[non_exhaustive]`, changing a trait's required method, or tightening a bound is breaking. Feature flags must be additive; a flag that removes API is a semver trap.
- **Arguments:** `&str` for borrowed text, `impl AsRef<Path>` for paths, `impl Into<String>` when you need ownership, `&[T]` over `&Vec<T>`.
- **Docs:** `#![warn(missing_docs)]`, a runnable example in the crate docs, and `# Errors` / `# Panics` sections. Doc tests keep examples honest.
- **`#[must_use]`** on results and builders catches ignored values at compile time.

Design the call site first. If the obvious call is wrong, the API is wrong.

questions.prompt: Why put `#[non_exhaustive]` on a public enum?
options: To allow adding variants without a breaking change
questions.explanation: Downstream matches must include a wildcard, so new variants are not breaking.

questions.explanation: It breaks every implementor, so it is a major change (or seal the trait).

questions.explanation: Callers can match on typed variants; anyhow belongs at the application edge.

lessons.title: Architecture and an unguided capstone

project.title: Build a supervised file-watcher daemon
project.description: No step-by-step lesson. Build a daemon that watches a directory, publishes JSON events on a Unix socket, keeps a small in-memory state, and shuts down cleanly. Acceptance: unit tests for the pure decision logic, an integration test over the socket, a systemd user unit, and a README. Read the brief in the lesson body for milestones and the rubric.

lessons.body:
Architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to change later. Three patterns carry most of the weight in this ecosystem.

**Pure core, effectful shell.** Put decisions in functions that take data and return data: a glob matcher, a state transition, a backoff policy, a freeze decision. The shell owns I/O, time, sockets and tasks. The core is fast to test and does not need a runtime.

**Ports and adapters.** The domain defines traits it needs (`Store`, `Clock`, `Notifier`); adapters implement them for SQLite, the real clock, or a socket. Dependencies point inward: the domain does not import the adapter. This is what lets `breadd` test adapters and normalisers without a compositor.

**One owner for mutable state.** Mutations travel as messages to a single consumer, which applies them in order. Readers get snapshots. This removes lock-order puzzles and makes the state machine inspectable.

Layer a workspace accordingly:

```
crates/shared     wire types, no I/O
crates/core       decisions, no I/O
crates/adapters   sockets, DB, compositor
crates/cli        argument parsing and exit codes
crates/daemon     wiring, supervision, shutdown
```

The capstone forces all of it: a `notify` watcher, an NDJSON Unix socket, a supervised task, graceful shutdown on SIGTERM, and tests that do not sleep.

**Rubric (aim for all six):**

1. The pure core has unit tests and no `async`.
2. The socket protocol has a version handshake and a tagged push message.
3. Backpressure is bounded; a slow client cannot grow memory without limit.
4. Shutdown drains in-flight work and exits zero.
5. A systemd user unit with `Restart=on-failure` and `WantedBy=default.target`.
6. A README that explains the protocol, the failure modes and how to run the tests.

If you get stuck, the earlier advanced lessons are the reference. Do not copy their examples; build the smallest version that passes each rubric item, then make it better.
